For example, at 1064 nm with w₀ = 0.5 mm, it is about 0.68 mrad. The wavefront is flat at the waist and becomes nearly spherical far away, with its radius of curvature at a minimum of 2zR at z = zR. In addition, passing through the waist, the beam acquires an extra phase of π relative to a plane wave, the Gouy phase. These properties are summarized in the complex beam parameter q = z + izR, whose changes can be calculated with ABCD matrices.

When a collimated beam of radius w is focused by a lens of focal length f, the waist radius is about λf/(πw). At 1.064 µm with w = 5 mm and f = 100 mm, it is about 6.8 µm. To shrink the spot, use a shorter focal length or enlarge the input beam with a beam expander. The depth of focus 2zR, however, becomes shallower in proportion to the square of the spot radius. Real beams depart from the ideal Gaussian, and the product of waist radius and divergence is M² times the ideal. In laser machining, beams with M² close to 1, such as those from fiber lasers, can combine a small spot with a long depth of focus.

faq.q: Where is the radius of a Gaussian beam measured?
faq.a: The radius at which the intensity falls to 1/e² (about 13.5%) of its center value is generally used. About 86% of the total power falls inside this circle. The full width at half maximum (FWHM) is also used, with FWHM ≈ 1.18w.

faq.q: How is the divergence of a Gaussian beam found?
faq.a: The far-field half-angle is θ = λ/(πw₀). The smaller the waist radius w₀, the more the beam spreads. For real beams, multiply by M²: θ = M²λ/(πw₀).

faq.q: How large is the spot when a beam is focused with a lens?
faq.a: When a collimated Gaussian beam (radius w) is focused by a lens of focal length f, the waist radius is about λf/(πw). Enlarging the input beam or shortening the focal length makes it smaller.

レイリー長.desc: The distance from the waist of a Gaussian beam to where the beam radius has grown by √2, zR = πw₀²/λ. A rough measure of the range over which the beam can be regarded as collimated.

about.p: The Rayleigh range zR = πw₀²/λ expresses how far from the waist a Gaussian beam stays narrow. At z = zR, the beam radius has grown by √2, the cross-sectional area has doubled, the center intensity has halved, and the wavefront radius of curvature is at its minimum of 2zR. The range ±zR around the waist (length 2zR) is called the confocal parameter and serves as a rough measure of where the beam can be regarded as collimated, that is, of the depth of focus. Beyond zR, the beam spreads linearly at the divergence angle λ/(πw₀) and can be regarded as the far field.

The Rayleigh range is proportional to the square of the waist radius and inversely proportional to the wavelength. At 1064 nm with w₀ = 0.5 mm, zR ≈ 0.74 m, but focusing to w₀ = 10 µm shortens it to about 0.3 mm. Halving the waist cuts the Rayleigh range to 1/4, so the depth of focus becomes sharply shallower for smaller spots. For the same waist radius, shorter-wavelength light has a longer Rayleigh range: twice as long for green (532 nm) as for 1064 nm. For real beams with M² greater than 1, zR = πw₀²/(M²λ), shorter by a factor of M².

about.h: How it is used in design
about.p: In laser machining, cutting thick material needs depth of focus, and making the spot too small leaves the Rayleigh range too short. The trade-off between spot size and Rayleigh range is set by the lens focal length and beam diameter. For coupling into optical fiber, a waist matching the fiber's mode is placed at the fiber end face. In resonator design, too, the waist and Rayleigh range follow from the condition that the mirror curvatures match the curvature of the beam's wavefront. In free-space optical communication and LiDAR, the transmitted beam is expanded to lengthen the Rayleigh range and limit spreading at a distance.

faq.q: What is the formula for the Rayleigh range?
faq.a: zR = πw₀²/λ (w₀ is the beam waist radius and λ the wavelength in the medium). For real beams, divide by M²: zR = πw₀²/(M²λ).

faq.q: How is the Rayleigh range related to the depth of focus?
faq.a: Within ±zR of the waist, the beam radius stays within √2 of its minimum. This length, 2zR (the confocal parameter), is often used as a rough measure of the depth of focus.

faq.q: What happens to the Rayleigh range when the spot is made smaller?
faq.a: It shortens in proportion to the square of the waist radius: halving the radius cuts the Rayleigh range to 1/4. A small spot and a long depth of focus are hard to achieve at the same time.

M².desc: The beam quality factor. It expresses how many times the product of a real beam's waist radius and divergence exceeds that of an ideal Gaussian beam. Values closer to 1 are better.

about.h: Beam quality in a single number
about.p: M² expresses how close a real laser beam is to an ideal Gaussian beam (TEM00) of the same wavelength. The product of the beam waist radius w₀ and the far-field divergence half-angle θ, called the beam parameter product (BPP), has its minimum value λ/π for an ideal Gaussian beam and equals M²λ/π for a real beam. M² is therefore always at least 1. At 1.064 µm, the BPP for M² = 1 is about 0.34 mm·mrad. The larger the M², the larger the focused spot for a beam of the same diameter.

M² cannot be found by measuring the beam diameter at a single position. The international standard ISO 11146 measures the diameter of a focused beam at no fewer than 10 positions, including points near the waist (within the Rayleigh range) and points far from it (beyond twice the Rayleigh range), and fits a curve of the form w(z)² = w₀² + (M²λ/(πw₀))²(z − z₀)². The beam diameter used is the D4σ diameter, calculated from the second moments of the intensity distribution. Diameters measured with knife-edge or slit methods can differ from the D4σ diameter depending on the profile shape.

Only a pure Gaussian beam has M² = 1; higher-order transverse modes have definite M² values. For Hermite–Gaussian modes TEMmn, for example, M² in the x direction is 2m + 1, so TEM10 has 3. Some beams, such as those of semiconductor lasers, have very different M² in the two transverse directions and are specified separately for each. Ideal lenses and mirrors leave M² unchanged, but lenses with aberrations, thermal lensing, and misaligned fiber coupling make it worse. Short of using a lossy spatial filter, no optical system can reduce M² afterward.

The radius of a focused spot is proportional to M², and for the same spot size the depth of focus becomes shallower in inverse proportion to M². Fine machining and long-distance propagation therefore call for beams with small M², and coupling into single-mode fiber is efficient only for beams with M² close to 1. Brightness, the power per unit area per unit solid angle, scales roughly as P/(M²λ)², so for the same output power doubling M² cuts brightness to about a quarter. Laser specifications state focusability as either M² or BPP.

faq.q: How are M² and BPP related?
faq.a: The beam parameter product (waist radius × divergence half-angle) equals M²λ/π. M² is dimensionless, with the wavelength divided out, whereas BPP has units such as mm·mrad; BPP is convenient when comparing the focusability of lasers with different wavelengths.

faq.q: How is M² measured?
faq.a: Focus the beam with a lens, measure the beam diameter (the second-moment D4σ diameter) at no fewer than 10 positions before and after the waist, and fit the propagation equation. The procedure is specified in ISO 11146. A diameter at a single position is not enough.

faq.q: Can M² be smaller than 1?
faq.a: No. The product of waist radius and divergence for an ideal Gaussian beam, λ/π, is the minimum allowed by diffraction. If a measurement gives less than 1, there may be a problem with the beam-diameter definition, the measurement positions, or the handling of background light.

Qスイッチ.desc: A method that holds the resonator loss high to store energy in the gain medium, then suddenly lowers the loss to release it, producing pulses of nanosecond order with high peak power.

about.h: Store energy, then release it all at once
about.p: Q-switching produces intense pulses by switching the cavity Q (how low its loss is) in time. If pumping continues while a high loss keeps the laser from oscillating, energy accumulates in the gain medium as a population inversion. When the loss is then lowered suddenly, the light is amplified explosively under gain far above threshold, and the stored energy comes out as a short pulse. Q-switching was demonstrated in the early 1960s and gives peak powers at the megawatt level with pulse widths on the order of nanoseconds. A 10 mJ, 10 ns pulse, for example, has a peak power of about 1 MW.

Active Q-switching switches the loss with an external signal. Electro-optic Q-switches using a Pockels cell switch quickly and suit high-energy pulses. Acousto-optic devices are commonly used to produce pulse trains at repetition rates from kilohertz to tens of kilohertz in continuously pumped lasers. Passive Q-switching places a saturable absorber such as Cr:YAG in the cavity; when the light grows strong enough to saturate the absorption, the loss drops automatically. It needs few components and can be made compact, but the pulse timing cannot be locked precisely to an external signal.

about.h: What sets the pulse width and energy
about.p: The pulse width of a Q-switched laser is set by the cavity round-trip time and the size of the gain, and it shortens as the cavity gets shorter. Microchip lasers, with cavities a few millimeters long, can produce pulses shorter than a nanosecond. The pulse energy is set by the energy that can be stored in the upper level, so materials with long upper-level lifetimes, such as Nd:YAG (about 230 µs), are well suited. Raising the repetition rate above the inverse of the lifetime reduces the energy stored per pulse, making the pulses weaker and longer. Semiconductor lasers, with their short lifetimes, are poorly suited to Q-switching.

about.h: Differences from other pulsing methods, and applications
about.p: Q-switching releases one large pulse at a time by switching the cavity loss, with typical pulse widths on the order of nanoseconds. Mode locking locks the phases of many longitudinal modes and instead delivers much shorter picosecond to femtosecond pulses at high repetition rates. Gain switching, which modulates the drive current of a semiconductor laser, is yet another, separate method. Taking advantage of their high peak power, Q-switched lasers are used for marking and micromachining, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, rangefinders, tattoo removal, and generating 532 nm green light by second-harmonic generation.

faq.q: How do you estimate the peak power of a Q-switched pulse?
faq.a: Divide the pulse energy by the pulse width for a rough value; 10 mJ in 10 ns gives about 1 MW. The exact value depends on the temporal pulse shape through a correction factor. The average power is the pulse energy multiplied by the repetition rate.

faq.q: What is the difference between active and passive Q-switching?
faq.a: Active Q-switching switches a Pockels cell or acousto-optic device with an external signal, so the pulse timing can be controlled. Passive Q-switching uses a saturable absorber that lowers the loss automatically as the light intensifies; it is simple and compact, but the timing jitters.

faq.q: Which laser materials are suited to Q-switching?
faq.a: Materials with long upper-level lifetimes that can store energy. Nd:YAG (about 230 µs), Nd:YVO₄, and Yb- or Er-based solid-state and fiber lasers are common. Semiconductor lasers, with carrier lifetimes on the order of nanoseconds, are not suited to Q-switching and use gain switching instead.

モード同期.desc: A method that locks the phases of many longitudinal modes to produce ultrashort pulses from picoseconds to femtoseconds. The repetition rate is the inverse of the resonator round-trip time, c/(2L).

about.h: Locking the phases of longitudinal modes
about.p: Mode locking produces short pulses by locking the phases of the many longitudinal modes oscillating simultaneously in a cavity, so that they interfere with one another. When evenly spaced modes add up in phase, they reinforce at one instant per cavity round trip and almost cancel in between. The result is a single pulse circulating in the cavity, with part of it extracted each time it reaches the output coupler. The pulse width is roughly the inverse of the total spectral width, so the more modes are locked, the shorter the pulse.

The repetition rate is the inverse of the round-trip time: c/(2L) for a linear cavity, and c divided by the optical length of one circuit for a ring cavity. A 2 m fiber ring (n = 1.47) gives about 100 MHz. The pulse width is set by the spectral width; for sech²-shaped pulses the time-bandwidth product is about 0.315, so a 100 fs pulse needs about 3.2 THz of bandwidth. A laser with 1 W average power at an 80 MHz repetition rate delivers 12.5 nJ per pulse, and at 100 fs the peak power reaches about 125 kW (a rough estimate treating the pulse as rectangular).

Active mode locking drives a modulator inside the cavity at a frequency equal to the mode spacing, forcing the mode phases into step. Passive mode locking uses a mechanism in which stronger light sees lower loss, so a short pulse develops by itself. Typical examples are semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors (SESAMs) and Kerr-lens mode locking, in which the Kerr effect focuses only intense light well; titanium-sapphire lasers have been reported to produce pulses shorter than 10 fs. Shorter pulses are more affected by cavity dispersion, which is compensated with prism pairs or chirped mirrors.

The repetition period and the pulse width are quite different things: a 100 MHz repetition rate only means a pulse arrives every 10 ns, while the pulse width is femtoseconds to picoseconds. Whereas Q-switching stores and releases energy, mode locking merely locks phases, so the energy in each pulse is small and is boosted by chirped-pulse amplification when needed. Mode-locked lasers are used for two-photon excitation microscopy, micromachining with reduced thermal effects, and time-resolved spectroscopy, and their evenly spaced longitudinal modes serve as optical frequency combs for precision frequency measurement.

faq.q: What sets the repetition rate of a mode-locked laser?
faq.a: The inverse of the time for light to make one round trip of the cavity: c/(2L) for a linear cavity in air, where L is the cavity length. It equals the longitudinal mode spacing. For the same average power, lengthening the cavity to lower the repetition rate increases the energy per pulse.

faq.q: What determines the pulse width in mode locking?
faq.a: The width of the phase-locked spectrum; the broader it is, the shorter the pulse. The time-bandwidth product (about 0.315 for sech² pulses) gives the lower bound. Materials with broad gain bandwidths, such as titanium sapphire, give shorter pulses, and dispersion compensation is also needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between mode locking and Q-switching?
faq.a: Q-switching switches the loss to release energy stored in the population inversion all at once, producing pulses on the order of nanoseconds. Mode locking locks the phases of longitudinal modes and delivers picosecond to femtosecond pulses at high repetition rates (roughly megahertz to gigahertz).

シングルモードファイバ.desc: An optical fiber that carries only the fundamental mode; for a step-index fiber, the condition is a V-number below 2.405. With no modal dispersion, it is used for long-distance, high-speed communication.

about.p: The number of modes guided in an optical fiber is set by the normalized frequency V = 2πaNA/λ (a is the core radius). For a step-index fiber, when V < 2.405 only the fundamental mode (LP01) propagates and the fiber is single-mode. Standard single-mode fiber has a core diameter of about 8 µm and an NA of about 0.12, with a cutoff wavelength designed to be 1.26 µm or below, so it is single-mode in the 1.31 µm and 1.55 µm bands. At shorter wavelengths such as 850 nm, higher-order modes also propagate. The fundamental mode has no cutoff, so it is guided even at small V, but the light spreads into the cladding and becomes sensitive to bending.

about.h: How it differs from multimode fiber
about.p: In multimode fiber (core diameter 50 µm or 62.5 µm) many modes propagate, each at a different speed, causing modal dispersion that spreads pulses. The product of distance and data rate is therefore limited, and multimode fiber is mainly used over short distances of a few hundred meters or less. Single-mode fiber has no modal dispersion; only chromatic dispersion and polarization mode dispersion remain, so transmission over tens to thousands of kilometers is possible. On the other hand, its small core means coupling to sources and other fibers needs micrometer-level alignment, raising component and assembly costs.

The main characteristics of standard single-mode fiber are a loss of about 0.2 dB/km at 1.55 µm and about 0.35 dB/km at 1.31 µm, and chromatic dispersion that is nearly zero around 1.31 µm and about 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1.55 µm. The mode field diameter is about 9.2 µm at 1.31 µm and about 10.4 µm at 1.55 µm, larger than the core diameter. Depending on the application, variants include dispersion-shifted fiber with zero dispersion moved to 1.55 µm, non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber that leaves a little dispersion, bend-insensitive fiber, large-core low-nonlinearity fiber, and polarization-maintaining fiber.

faq.q: What is the difference between single-mode and multimode fiber?
faq.a: Single-mode fiber carries only the fundamental mode and has no modal dispersion, so it is used for long-distance, high-speed communication. Multimode fiber has a thick core that carries many modes, making connections easier, but modal dispersion limits the distance.

faq.q: What is the condition for single-mode operation?
faq.a: For a step-index fiber, V = 2πaNA/λ < 2.405. The shortest wavelength satisfying this condition is the cutoff wavelength, and the fiber is single-mode at longer wavelengths.

faq.q: Can 850 nm light be used in single-mode fiber?
faq.a: In standard single-mode fiber, 850 nm is shorter than the cutoff wavelength, so higher-order modes also propagate and the fiber is not strictly single-mode. It can be used over short distances, but issues such as modal noise arise.

V値.desc: The normalized frequency of an optical fiber, V = 2πaNA/λ. It indicates roughly how many modes propagate; a step-index fiber is single-mode when V is below 2.405.

about.h: Fiber properties in a single number
about.p: The V-number (normalized frequency) is a dimensionless number defined for step-index optical fiber as V = 2πaNA/λ = (2πa/λ)√(n₁² − n₂²), where a is the core radius. It combines three conditions, core size, index difference, and wavelength, into one, so fibers with the same V have guided modes of the same shape and number even if their dimensions or wavelengths differ. Many fiber properties, including the strength of confinement, the number of guided modes, the mode field diameter, and bend sensitivity, can be organized and compared in terms of V.

about.h: Single-mode condition and number of modes
about.p: In step-index fiber, only the fundamental mode (LP01) propagates when V < 2.405. The value 2.405 is the first zero of the zeroth-order Bessel function and is the cutoff of the next mode, LP11. As V grows further, LP21 and LP02 begin to propagate at 3.832. In multimode fiber with large V, the number of modes is roughly V²/2. For example, sending 850 nm light through step-index fiber with a 50 µm core diameter and NA 0.2 gives V ≈ 37 and about 680 modes. Graded-index fiber with a parabolic profile supports roughly half as many.

about.h: The problem with too small a V
about.p: The fundamental mode has no cutoff, so light is guided however small V becomes. If V is too small, however, light spreads far into the cladding, confinement weakens, and even slight bends increase loss. For this reason, standard single-mode fiber is designed to have V of around 2 at its operating wavelength. Because V is inversely proportional to wavelength, the same fiber becomes multimode at shorter wavelengths where V exceeds 2.405. The wavelength at which V = 2.405 is the cutoff wavelength, and at wavelengths above it the fiber is single-mode.

The V-number also makes it easy to estimate the mode field diameter. Marcuse's formula based on the Gaussian approximation, w/a ≈ 0.65 + 1.619V^(−1.5) + 2.879V^(−6), where w is the mode field radius, fits well over the single-mode range (V of roughly 1.2 to 2.4) and is used to estimate splice losses. A similar normalized frequency is defined for planar waveguides and gives a guide to the thickness or width for single-mode operation. Some photonic crystal fibers, which have arrays of air holes, keep an effective V nearly constant regardless of wavelength and remain single-mode over a wide wavelength range.

faq.q: How do you calculate the V-number?
faq.a: V = 2πaNA/λ, where a is the core radius (not the diameter), NA is the numerical aperture, and λ is the vacuum wavelength. Since NA = √(n₁² − n₂²), it can also be calculated directly from the refractive indices. Using the core diameter gives a value twice too large.

faq.q: What does the value 2.405 mean for the V-number?
faq.a: It is the value of V at which the second mode (LP11) begins to propagate in step-index fiber, corresponding to the first zero of the zeroth-order Bessel function J₀. Below it, only the fundamental mode propagates and the fiber is single-mode.

faq.q: How is the V-number related to the number of modes?
faq.a: Below 2.405 there is only the fundamental mode, and as V grows more modes propagate. In step-index fiber with sufficiently large V, the number of modes is roughly V²/2, so doubling V gives about four times as many modes.

モードフィールド径.desc: The diameter at which the intensity of light guided in a single-mode fiber falls to 1/e². It is larger than the core diameter, grows at longer wavelengths, and governs splice loss.

about.h: How far the light actually spreads
about.p: The fundamental mode of single-mode fiber is not confined to the core alone; it extends into the cladding. The mode field diameter (MFD) expresses how widely the light actually spreads, defined, when the intensity profile is approximated as Gaussian, as the diameter at which the intensity falls to 1/e² of its center value. In standard single-mode fiber with a core diameter of about 8 µm, the MFD is about 9.2 µm at 1310 nm and about 10.4 µm at 1550 nm, larger than the core. Splice and coupling losses are set by the MFD, not the core diameter.

As wavelength increases, the V-number decreases, confinement weakens, and the MFD grows. Marcuse's approximation w/a ≈ 0.65 + 1.619V^(−1.5) + 2.879V^(−6), where w is the mode field radius and a is the core radius, estimates that fiber with a 4.1 µm core radius and NA 0.12 has an MFD of about 9.1 µm at 1310 nm (V ≈ 2.36) and about 10.4 µm at 1550 nm (V ≈ 1.99). The smaller V becomes, the faster the MFD grows, and the more easily light leaks out of the cladding when the fiber is bent.

Two fibers with different MFDs lose light even when butted together with their axes aligned, because the mode sizes do not match. In the Gaussian approximation the coupling efficiency is (2w₁w₂/(w₁² + w₂²))², which gives about 0.3 dB for fibers with MFDs of 10.4 µm and 8.0 µm. When such a splice is measured with an OTDR, the loss can appear negative from one direction (an apparent gain), so it is measured from both directions and averaged. A larger MFD also increases the effective area of the light and lowers its intensity, making nonlinear effects less likely.

The MFD is a basic quantity in fusion splicing between fibers, coupling to lasers and waveguides, and connector design. Modes in silicon waveguides are small, under 1 µm, so spot-size converters and lensed fibers are used to bridge the difference from the fiber MFD. Long-haul systems that need to suppress nonlinear effects use fibers with an enlarged effective area, while bend-insensitive fibers have a slightly smaller MFD. The MFD is evaluated by methods such as measuring the far-field intensity distribution of the light leaving the fiber and calculating it from that.

faq.q: What is the difference between mode field diameter and core diameter?
faq.a: The core diameter is the diameter of the high-index region, while the mode field diameter is the diameter over which the light intensity falls to 1/e² of its center value. Because light extends into the cladding, the MFD of single-mode fiber is larger than its core, and splice loss is set by the MFD.

faq.q: How much loss occurs when splicing fibers with different mode field diameters?
faq.a: Estimate it with the Gaussian coupling efficiency (2w₁w₂/(w₁² + w₂²))². For MFDs of 10.4 µm and 8.0 µm, the loss is about 0.3 dB. Any lateral offset or angular misalignment adds its own loss on top.

faq.q: Why does the mode field diameter grow with wavelength?
faq.a: A longer wavelength lowers the V-number (2πaNA/λ), which weakens the confinement of light in the core and lets more of it extend into the cladding. In standard fiber, the MFD grows by about 1 µm from 1310 nm to 1550 nm.

波長分散.desc: The phenomenon in which the group velocity of light depends on wavelength, so optical pulses spread as they propagate. It is the sum of material and waveguide dispersion, expressed in ps/(nm·km).

about.p: An optical pulse has a finite spectral width and contains components at many wavelengths. If the group velocity in the fiber depends on wavelength, the components arrive at different times and the pulse spreads. This is chromatic dispersion. Its size is expressed by the dispersion parameter D, and the pulse spreading is Δτ = D × L × Δλ. For example, D = 17 ps/(nm·km), 50 km and a spectral width of 0.1 nm give 85 ps. Dispersion is the sum of material dispersion, from the wavelength dependence of silica's refractive index, and waveguide dispersion, from the way confinement of light in the core changes with wavelength; in standard single-mode fiber the two cancel near 1.31 µm, giving zero.

Pulses spread by chromatic dispersion overlap neighboring bits and cause errors through intersymbol interference. The dispersion limit tightens roughly in inverse proportion to the square of the bit rate, so going from 10 Gb/s to 40 Gb/s cuts the allowed distance to about 1/16. Sources with wider spectra (multimode lasers, or chirp from direct modulation) are affected more, so long-haul systems combine narrow-linewidth DFB lasers with external modulators. Short-reach systems with intensity modulation and direct detection use the 1.31 µm band (O band), where dispersion is nearly zero, to avoid the need for dispersion compensation.

Ways to suppress the effects of dispersion include dispersion-compensating fiber with large dispersion of the opposite sign, chirped fiber Bragg gratings, and electronic compensation by digital signal processing at the receiver. In coherent communication, the phase of the received field can be measured too, so dispersion from thousands of kilometers can be compensated with digital filters. Dispersion is not all bad: in wavelength-multiplexed transmission, zero dispersion keeps the phases of the wavelengths aligned and strengthens four-wave mixing, so non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber that leaves a little dispersion is used. In ultrashort-pulse lasers, prism pairs and chirped mirrors compensate dispersion to shorten the pulses.

faq.q: How is pulse spreading from chromatic dispersion calculated?
faq.a: Δτ = D × L × Δλ, where D is the dispersion parameter (ps/(nm·km)), L the distance (km) and Δλ the spectral width of the light (nm). For standard single-mode fiber at 1.55 µm, D ≈ 17 ps/(nm·km).

faq.q: Why is 1.31 µm used for short-reach optical communication?
faq.a: Because the chromatic dispersion of standard single-mode fiber is nearly zero around 1.31 µm, so even high-speed signals barely spread. The loss is larger than at 1.55 µm, but that is not a problem over short distances.

faq.q: What is the difference between chromatic dispersion and polarization mode dispersion?
faq.a: Chromatic dispersion is spreading from the wavelength dependence of group velocity; it grows in proportion to distance and is a fixed quantity that is easy to compensate. Polarization mode dispersion comes from the group-velocity difference between two polarizations; it grows with the square root of distance and changes over time with temperature and vibration.

偏波モード分散.desc: The difference in group velocity between the two polarization modes caused by slight birefringence in a fiber. The delay difference grows with the square root of distance and fluctuates over time.

about.h: A difference in arrival time between two polarizations
about.p: In single-mode fiber with a perfectly circular core, the two orthogonal polarizations travel at the same speed. In practice, however, slight core ellipticity, internal stress, bending, and twisting create weak birefringence, and the group velocities of the two polarizations differ. As a result, the two polarization components of an optical pulse arrive at different times (the differential group delay, DGD), and the pulse spreads out in time. This is polarization mode dispersion (PMD), and the pair of polarizations with the smallest and largest delays are called the principal states of polarization.

about.h: Why it scales with the square root of distance
about.p: In long fibers, the orientation and size of the birefringence change randomly along the length, and energy keeps exchanging between the two polarizations. The delay difference therefore adds and subtracts section by section in a random walk, and the mean DGD grows with the square root of distance. This is why the PMD coefficient has units of ps/√km. In short fibers with fixed axes, or in polarization-maintaining fiber, the delay difference grows in proportion to distance instead. The DGD fluctuates over time following a Maxwellian distribution, and the probability of exceeding three times the mean is about 4×10⁻⁵.

about.h: Impact on transmission and rules of thumb
about.p: For intensity-modulated signals, a common rule of thumb is that the effect is small if the mean DGD is within about 10% of the bit period. At 10 Gb/s this means 10% of 100 ps, or 10 ps, so for fiber with a PMD coefficient of 0.5 ps/√km the limit is roughly (10/0.5)² = 400 km. Current standards for single-mode fiber (such as ITU-T G.652.D) require a link design value of 0.2 ps/√km or less. PMD changes from moment to moment with temperature, vibration, and wind swaying aerial cables, which sets it apart from the fixed chromatic dispersion; it cannot be cancelled by a fixed compensator.

Methods for measuring PMD include deriving the delay from Jones matrices measured at two closely spaced wavelengths and methods using interferometers. In higher-order PMD, the principal states of polarization themselves vary with wavelength and combine with chromatic dispersion to distort waveforms further. Countermeasures are essential at 40 Gb/s and above, and in today's digital coherent transmission, digital signal processing at the receiver adaptively tracks and compensates polarization rotation and DGD. Polarization-dependent loss (PDL), a difference in loss between polarizations, is a separate phenomenon from PMD and should not be confused with it.

faq.q: Why is the PMD coefficient given in ps/√km?
faq.a: In long fibers the birefringence axes change randomly, so the delay difference adds and subtracts section by section in a random walk and the mean delay grows with the square root of distance. Multiplying the coefficient by the square root of the distance in kilometers gives the mean DGD.

faq.q: What is the difference between polarization mode dispersion and chromatic dispersion?
faq.a: Chromatic dispersion arises because group velocity depends on wavelength; its value is fixed, so it can be cancelled with dispersion-compensating fiber and similar means. Polarization mode dispersion comes from the group-velocity difference between two polarizations and changes over time with temperature and vibration, so it requires adaptive compensation.

faq.q: How is PMD compensated?
faq.a: Today's coherent receivers estimate the mixing of the two polarizations and the delay between them with digital signal processing and cancel them adaptively. In earlier intensity-modulation systems, the remedies were choosing low-PMD fiber and using optical compensators.

EDFA.desc: An erbium-doped fiber amplifier. Pumped at 980 nm or 1480 nm, it amplifies many wavelengths in the 1.55 µm band at once without converting the light back to electricity.

about.h: An amplifier that works on light directly
about.p: An EDFA sends light from a semiconductor pump laser, together with the signal, into a fiber a few meters to a few tens of meters long whose core is doped with erbium ions (Er³⁺); the pump creates a population inversion that amplifies 1.55 µm signals by stimulated emission. Practical forms were demonstrated in the late 1980s and replaced repeaters that converted light back into electrical signals for regeneration. Because it amplifies many wavelengths within its band at once, it is the core technology that made high-capacity, long-haul transmission with wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) possible.

Pumping uses either 980 nm or 1480 nm. A 980 nm pump excites a level above the signal levels, which makes a nearly complete inversion easier and allows a low noise figure. A 1480 nm pump excites the top of the same band of levels as the signal directly and loses little photon energy, so its quantum-limited conversion efficiency for a 1550 nm signal is about 95%, higher than the roughly 63% of 980 nm pumping. The basic amplification band is the C band (about 1530 to 1565 nm), and L-band EDFAs (about 1565 to 1625 nm) use longer fiber.

Gain is about 20 to 40 dB depending on the application, and the practical noise figure is about 4 to 6 dB, larger than the quantum limit of about 3 dB. Spontaneous emission is amplified along with the signal and becomes noise (ASE), which accumulates over cascaded amplifiers and lowers the optical signal-to-noise ratio. Gain is not flat across wavelength, so WDM systems correct it with gain-flattening filters. The upper-level lifetime of erbium is long, about 10 ms, so the gain does not follow Gb/s signal variations and crosstalk between wavelengths is small; but a sudden change in the number of channels shifts the power of the remaining ones, so automatic gain control is needed.

Depending on where they sit, EDFAs are boosters that raise output power just after the transmitter, in-line amplifiers that make up for loss partway along the link, or preamplifiers that improve sensitivity just before the receiver. In long-haul terrestrial and submarine systems, EDFAs are placed every few tens of kilometers up to about 100 km. Inside are WDM couplers that combine pump and signal, and optical isolators that prevent oscillation from back-reflections. The 1.3 µm band cannot be amplified by erbium, so praseodymium-doped fiber amplifiers or semiconductor optical amplifiers are used there.

faq.q: Why are 980 nm and 1480 nm used to pump EDFAs?
faq.a: Because both are wavelengths that erbium ions absorb. A 980 nm pump makes a complete inversion easier and gives a lower noise figure, while a 1480 nm pump has a smaller photon-energy difference from the signal and so a higher conversion efficiency; they are chosen according to the application.

faq.q: Which wavelength bands can EDFAs amplify?
faq.a: Mainly the C band (about 1530 to 1565 nm), and with longer erbium-doped fiber the L band (about 1565 to 1625 nm) as well. The 1.3 µm band cannot be amplified, so other types of amplifiers are used there.

faq.q: What is the noise figure of an EDFA?
faq.a: It is the ratio of the input to the output signal-to-noise ratio, expressed in dB, and shows how much noise amplification adds. The quantum limit for high gain and complete inversion is about 3 dB, and practical EDFAs are around 4 to 6 dB.

応答度.desc: The photocurrent (A/W) produced when 1 W of light enters a photodetector. Set by wavelength and quantum efficiency: R = ηqλ/(hc) ≈ η × λ[µm]/1.24.

about.p: Responsivity R is the ratio of photocurrent I to optical power P, R = I/P, in A/W. Using the quantum efficiency η (the number of electrons generated and collected per incident photon), R = ηqλ/(hc). In practice R ≈ η × λ[µm] / 1.24, so even an ideal detector with 100% quantum efficiency is limited to about 0.69 A/W at 850 nm, about 1.06 A/W at 1310 nm and about 1.25 A/W at 1550 nm. Quantum efficiency is a ratio of numbers of particles and can be compared across wavelengths, while responsivity is the current conversion factor used in circuit design.

With constant quantum efficiency, responsivity increases in proportion to wavelength, because the same 1 W of light at a longer wavelength has lower energy per photon and therefore more photons. A real responsivity curve falls at short wavelengths, where light is absorbed near the surface and lost to recombination, and drops sharply at long wavelengths near the cutoff set by the band gap, where absorption weakens. Silicon peaks around 0.9 µm and hardly detects wavelengths beyond 1.1 µm. InGaAs is sensitive up to about 1.65 µm and Ge up to about 1.8 µm (Ge's sensitivity falls steeply beyond 1.6 µm).

Quantum efficiency is the product of the fraction of light that gets past the surface (not reflected), the fraction absorbed in the absorption layer, and the efficiency of collecting the generated carriers at the electrodes. An anti-reflection coating suppresses surface reflection of tens of percent, a thick absorption layer absorbs the light fully, and a high-field depletion region collects carriers before they recombine. A thick absorption layer, however, lengthens the transit time and lowers the bandwidth, so high-speed detectors use waveguide structures or back-side reflection to secure a long absorption length with a thin absorption layer. In an APD, internal multiplication raises the apparent responsivity by the gain M, but the quantum efficiency itself does not increase.

faq.q: What is the formula for responsivity?
faq.a: R = ηqλ/(hc) ≈ η × λ[µm] / 1.24 [A/W]. For example, 80% quantum efficiency gives about 1.0 A/W at 1.55 µm and about 0.55 A/W at 850 nm.

faq.q: What is the difference between responsivity and quantum efficiency?
faq.a: Quantum efficiency is the number of electrons per photon, a dimensionless ratio. Responsivity is the current per watt of optical power (A/W); because photon energy depends on wavelength, the same quantum efficiency gives higher responsivity at longer wavelengths.

faq.q: Can responsivity exceed 1 A/W?
faq.a: Even at 100% quantum efficiency, it exceeds 1 A/W for wavelengths longer than 1.24 µm (about 1.25 A/W at 1.55 µm). Devices with internal multiplication, such as APDs, can raise the apparent responsivity many times further.

APD.desc: An avalanche photodiode: a photodetector that multiplies the photocurrent internally by avalanche multiplication under high reverse bias. It adds excess noise.

about.h: A photodetector with internal current gain
about.p: An APD (avalanche photodiode) is a photodetector operated at a high reverse bias close to breakdown, where carriers generated by light are accelerated by the strong field and cause impact ionization, multiplying electron–hole pairs in an avalanche. Because the photocurrent is multiplied internally by a factor M (the multiplication gain), the signal becomes large relative to the thermal noise of the following amplifier, making weak light easier to receive. Gains range from a few to several hundred, and some silicon APDs exceed 100. APDs are used in telecom receivers, lidar, and radiation detection.

Avalanche multiplication is a random process, so the gain fluctuates and shot noise grows by even more than M². The additional factor is the excess noise factor F, given by McIntyre's formula F = kM + (1 − k)(2 − 1/M). Here k is the ratio of the impact-ionization rates of electrons and holes, and the smaller it is, the lower the noise. At M = 10, F ≈ 2 for silicon with k ≈ 0.02, and F ≈ 6 for InP with k ≈ 0.5. That is why silicon APDs are low-noise, while InGaAs/InP APDs are often run at a gain of around 10.

Raising the gain increases the signal but also the excess noise, so the optimum gain is set by the balance between thermal noise and multiplication noise. When shot noise dominates, multiplication does not improve the SNR and actually degrades it by the excess noise. Telecom InGaAs/InP APDs separate the InGaAs layer that absorbs light from the InP layer that provides multiplication (the SAM structure), avoiding high fields across the narrow-gap layer that would increase tunneling current. Speed is limited by the time needed for the avalanche to build up, and the product of gain and bandwidth tends to stay roughly constant.

about.h: Differences from PIN photodiodes and SPADs, and practical use
about.p: A PIN photodiode has no internal gain (gain of 1), so in receivers dominated by thermal noise its sensitivity is limited. An APD can improve receiver sensitivity by a few dB over a PIN. A single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) is operated above breakdown so that even a single photon produces a large pulse, an operating regime different from that of an APD. The breakdown voltage of an APD changes with temperature, and the gain at a fixed voltage then changes greatly, so circuits that adjust the bias voltage to the temperature are needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between an APD and a PIN photodiode?
faq.a: An APD causes avalanche multiplication at high reverse bias and multiplies the photocurrent internally; a PIN has no multiplication. An APD can raise sensitivity in receivers dominated by thermal noise, but it has excess noise and needs a high voltage and temperature control.

faq.q: What gain should an APD be operated at?
faq.a: At the optimum set by the balance between thermal noise and excess noise. InGaAs/InP APDs are typically run at around 10, and silicon APDs, with their low excess noise, often at several tens up to about 100. Too high a gain increases noise and actually worsens sensitivity.

faq.q: What is the excess noise factor?
faq.a: It is the factor by which fluctuations in avalanche gain make shot noise grow beyond the square of the gain. It is given by McIntyre's formula F = kM + (1 − k)(2 − 1/M), and it is smaller for materials with a smaller ratio k of electron and hole ionization rates.

ショット雑音.desc: Noise from charge arriving randomly as discrete particles. The rms current is √(2qIB), proportional to the square roots of the average current I and the bandwidth B.

about.h: Noise from the graininess of charge
about.p: Shot noise is the fluctuation in current that arises because the electrons carrying it arrive one by one at random times. Schottky analyzed it in vacuum tubes in 1918. When arrivals follow Poisson statistics, the rms noise current is i = √(2qIB), where q is the elementary charge, I the mean current, and B the bandwidth, and the noise is white, independent of frequency. In photodetection, the arrival of photons is itself random, so shot noise cannot be avoided even with an ideal detector; it is also called quantum noise.

For a mean current of 1 µA and a bandwidth of 1 MHz, the noise current is √(2 × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁶) ≈ 0.57 nA. The (power) signal-to-noise ratio is I²/(2qIB) = I/(2qB), about 65 dB in this example. Because shot noise grows with the square root of the current, its share relative to the signal shrinks as the current increases, and in a receiver dominated by shot noise the SNR rises in proportion to optical power. In terms of photons, counting an average of N photons gives a fluctuation of √N.

about.h: How it differs from thermal noise
about.p: Thermal noise in a resistor is set by temperature T and resistance R even with no current flowing, with a noise current of √(4kTB/R). Shot noise appears only when current flows and does not depend on temperature. With a 50 Ω load at 300 K, the two are equal when the photocurrent is 2kT/(qR) ≈ 1 mA, and below that current thermal noise dominates. Also, for current through an ordinary metal resistor, shot noise is strongly suppressed; the noise given by this formula appears when carriers cross a barrier independently, as in a pn junction or a vacuum tube.

about.h: Measurements that aim for the shot-noise limit
about.p: Precision optical measurements aim for a condition in which thermal noise and laser intensity noise are suppressed and only shot noise remains (the shot-noise limit). Balanced detection, which takes the difference between two photodetectors, is a typical way to cancel laser intensity noise and approach the shot-noise limit. In coherent detection, mixing in a strong local oscillator amplifies the signal so that the shot noise of the local oscillator dominates the receiver's thermal noise. Getting noise below the shot-noise level, however, requires quantum states of light such as squeezed light.

faq.q: How do you calculate shot noise?
faq.a: The rms noise current is √(2qIB), with q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, I the mean current, and B the receiver bandwidth. For 1 µA and 1 MHz, for example, it is about 0.57 nA. Dark current also produces shot noise, so include the sum of photocurrent and dark current in I.

faq.q: What is the difference between shot noise and thermal noise?
faq.a: Shot noise arises from current flow and grows with the square root of the current. Thermal noise comes from the thermal motion of electrons in a resistor and is set by temperature and resistance, independent of current. Thermal noise dominates at small photocurrents and shot noise at large ones.

faq.q: How does SNR depend on optical power at the shot-noise limit?
faq.a: SNR is proportional to optical power, because signal power goes as the square of the current while shot-noise power goes as the current. Doubling the optical power doubles the SNR (about 3 dB). When thermal noise dominates, it increases fourfold (about 6 dB).

NEP.desc: Noise-equivalent power: the incident optical power at which signal equals noise, in W/√Hz. The smaller it is, the weaker the light that can be detected.

about.h: How weak a signal can be detected
about.p: NEP (noise-equivalent power) is the incident optical power at which the signal and noise at the detector output are exactly equal (an SNR of 1), expressed per 1 Hz of bandwidth in units of W/√Hz. It is found by dividing the noise current density (A/√Hz) by the responsivity (A/W). The smaller the NEP, the weaker the light that can be detected. A rough minimum detectable power in bandwidth B is NEP × √B, which worsens in proportion to √B as the bandwidth widens. It is the basic figure for comparing sensitivity on photodetector datasheets.

For a photodiode with 10 pA of dark current, if the only noise is the shot noise of that dark current, the noise current density is √(2qId) ≈ 1.8×10⁻¹⁵ A/√Hz. Dividing by a responsivity of 0.6 A/W gives an NEP of about 3×10⁻¹⁵ W/√Hz. In a 1 kHz bandwidth, the minimum detectable power is then about 3×10⁻¹⁵ × √1000, or roughly 1×10⁻¹³ W. In a real circuit, however, the feedback resistor and amplifier add noise, and the system NEP is often larger than this, so it should be kept distinct from the NEP of the device itself.

about.h: How it differs from D*, and points to watch
about.p: NEP depends on the size of the active area, so detectors of different area are compared using the specific detectivity D* = √(AB)/NEP, where A is the active area. Its unit is cm·√Hz/W, also called the Jones, and unlike NEP, a larger value is better. NEP depends on wavelength through the responsivity and, depending on the frequency spectrum of the noise, on the measurement frequency as well. When a datasheet gives NEP in W rather than W/√Hz, it is a value for a specific bandwidth, so check the units carefully.

For measuring weak light, choose a detector with a small NEP and narrow the bandwidth to what is needed. Averaging a measurement over a time T gives an equivalent noise bandwidth of about 1/(2T), so a 0.5 second average corresponds to a 1 Hz bandwidth and the NEP value itself becomes the estimate of the minimum detectable power. Infrared detectors are cooled to reduce dark current and background radiation and thereby lower their NEP. But NEP is not the only factor: the maximum measurable power (dynamic range), response speed, and active area must also be considered.

faq.q: Why is NEP given in W/√Hz?
faq.a: Noise current grows with the square root of bandwidth, √B, so NEP is expressed per √Hz as a value independent of bandwidth. The minimum detectable power in bandwidth B is found by multiplying the NEP by √B.

faq.q: What is the difference between NEP and D*?
faq.a: NEP is the optical power at which signal equals noise, and smaller is better. D* (specific detectivity) is normalized to active area and bandwidth as √(AB)/NEP, and larger is better. D* is suited to comparing detectors of different area.

faq.q: How is NEP determined?
faq.a: Divide the detector's noise current density (A/√Hz) by its responsivity (A/W) at the wavelength of interest. If the only noise is the shot noise of the dark current, NEP = √(2qId)/R. When thermal or amplifier noise is present, use the total noise combined as a root sum of squares.

暗電流.desc: The current that flows in a photodetector with no light. Caused by thermal generation and leakage, it increases with temperature and is a source of noise.

about.h: Current that flows even without light
about.p: Dark current is the current that flows in a photodetector when no light falls on it. Its main components are generation current, from electron–hole pairs created thermally in the depletion region; diffusion current, from carriers diffusing in from the neutral regions outside it; surface leakage current along the surfaces and sidewalls of the device; and tunneling current, from carriers passing through the band gap under strong fields. Dark current not only adds an error to the signal; its shot noise sets the limit for detecting weak light, making it an important property of a photodetector. It matters especially in infrared detection and long exposures, where the signal photocurrent is small.

Generation and diffusion currents come from thermal excitation across the band gap, so they rise steeply with temperature. Generation current scales roughly as exp(−Eg/2kT) and diffusion current roughly as exp(−Eg/kT), and raising silicon from 25 °C to 35 °C increases them by about 2 and about 4 times, respectively, by calculation. Doubling for every 10 °C rise is a common rule of thumb for silicon photodiodes. Materials with smaller band gaps have larger dark currents, so for the same area dark current tends to increase in the order Si, InGaAs, Ge.

It is tempting to think dark current can simply be subtracted from the measurement. A constant dark current can be subtracted, but its shot noise, √(2qIdB), is a random fluctuation that cannot be subtracted and remains on top of the signal. Dark current also changes strongly with temperature, so if the temperature drifts, the value to subtract changes too. The components also scale differently with size: generation and diffusion currents are roughly proportional to the active area, and surface leakage to the perimeter, so comparing devices of different size reveals which component dominates.

The basics of suppressing dark current are cooling and choice of bias. Infrared detectors and scientific image sensors cooled with Peltier elements operate with far smaller dark current than at room temperature. Lowering the reverse bias narrows the depletion region and reduces dark current, and at zero bias dark current is nearly zero, which suits precise low-frequency optical power measurement. Improving the passivation layer on the surface of the device is also effective. Image sensors, for their part, correct for dark current using light-shielded pixels or frames taken in the dark.

faq.q: Why does dark current increase with temperature?
faq.a: Because its main components come from electrons being thermally excited across the band gap. The probability of this rises exponentially with temperature, and for silicon photodiodes a common rule of thumb is that dark current roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise.

faq.q: How can dark current be reduced?
faq.a: Methods include cooling the device, lowering the reverse bias to only what is needed, reducing the active area, and improving surface passivation. At zero bias dark current is nearly zero, but the junction capacitance becomes larger and the response slower.

faq.q: Are dark current and dark-current noise different?
faq.a: Yes. Dark current itself can be subtracted if it is constant, but the shot noise it produces, √(2qIdB), is a random fluctuation and cannot be subtracted. In weak-light detection, this shot noise sets the NEP. Datasheet values should be read together with their bias and temperature conditions.

リング共振器.desc: A device in which light circulating in a looped waveguide resonates when the round-trip optical path is an integer number of wavelengths. Its FSR is λ²/(n_g L). Used for filters and modulators.

about.p: A ring resonator places a bus waveguide next to a looped waveguide so that part of the light transfers into the ring by evanescent coupling. At wavelengths where the phase acquired in one round trip is an integer multiple of 2π, that is, n_eff × L = mλ (L is the circumference), the circulating light builds up and resonates. The wavelength spacing to the next resonance (the FSR) uses the group index n_g, which includes dispersion: FSR = λ²/(n_gL). For a silicon ring with a radius of 10 µm and a group index of 4.2, it is about 9.1 nm at 1550 nm. The FSR is widened by shrinking the ring, but bending loss increases, so a radius of a few micrometers is roughly the lower limit in silicon.

The sharpness of resonance is expressed by Q = λ/Δλ (Δλ is the full width at half maximum), which depends on both the loss inside the ring and the strength of coupling to the bus waveguide. A linewidth of 0.05 nm at 1550 nm gives a Q of about 3.1×10⁴. At critical coupling, where the coupling equals the round-trip loss, the through-port transmission at the resonance wavelength is zero, giving deep extinction. With overcoupling the linewidth broadens, and with undercoupling the extinction is shallow. Adding a second waveguide as a drop port makes a wavelength demultiplexer (add-drop filter) that extracts only the resonant wavelength.

Ring resonators are used as filters for wavelength multiplexing and demultiplexing, as ring modulators, as sensors, and for generating optical frequency combs through nonlinear optics. Ring modulators are small with low capacitance, so they run fast at low power, and rings with different resonance wavelengths can be lined up along one bus waveguide to build multiwavelength transmitters. On the other hand, silicon's thermo-optic coefficient is large, about 1.8×10⁻⁴ /K, and the resonance moves by about 0.07 nm/K, so heater tuning and feedback temperature control are essential. Even nanometer-level variations in waveguide width and thickness shift the resonance wavelength, so designs assume post-fabrication tuning.

faq.q: How is the FSR of a ring resonator calculated?
faq.a: FSR = λ²/(n_gL), where L is the ring circumference (2πR) and n_g is the group index. Using the effective index instead gives large errors in highly dispersive waveguides such as silicon wires, so take care.

faq.q: What is the Q of a ring resonator?
faq.a: It is the resonance wavelength divided by the full width at half maximum of the resonance and expresses how sharp the resonance is. It also corresponds to the time photons stay in the ring, τ = Qλ/(2πc); a higher Q gives a sharper filter but greater sensitivity to temperature changes.

faq.q: Why do ring resonators need heaters?
faq.a: Because silicon's refractive index changes strongly with temperature, shifting the resonance wavelength by about 0.07 nm/K. Heaters and control are used to tune the resonance to the operating wavelength, including shifts from fabrication variation, and to hold it there as temperature changes.

群屈折率.desc: The index that describes the speed at which light pulses and energy travel (the group velocity), n_g = n_eff − λ dn_eff/dλ. Used to calculate FSR and delay times.

方向性結合器.desc: A splitter that brings two waveguides close together and transfers light by evanescent coupling. The coupling length sets the split ratio, and half the full coupling length gives a 3 dB split.

MMIカプラ.desc: A splitting and combining element that uses self-imaging in a wide multimode waveguide. Its split ratio tends to stay stable against fabrication variation and wavelength.

熱光学効果.desc: The change of refractive index with temperature. Silicon's is large, about 1.8×10⁻⁴ /K, and is used to tune phase and resonance wavelength with heaters.

グレーティングカプラ.desc: A periodic structure etched into a waveguide that couples light to a fiber above the chip. Its period is set by the phase-matching condition Λ = λ/(n_eff − sinθ).

dBm.desc: A logarithmic expression of power referenced to 1 mW, 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW). 0 dBm is 1 mW, 10 dBm is 10 mW and −30 dBm is 1 µW.

OTDR.desc: An instrument that launches light pulses into a fiber and measures the distribution of loss and the positions of splices and breaks from the round-trip time and strength of backscattered and reflected light.

LiDAR.desc: A technique that illuminates objects with laser light and measures their distance and shape from the reflections. Methods include ToF, which times pulse round trips, and FMCW, which uses frequency sweeps.

OCT.desc: Optical coherence tomography: interferometry using the short coherence length of broadband light to image the depth structure of tissue with micrometer-level resolution.

第2高調波発生.desc: The second-order nonlinear optical process that produces light at twice the frequency, 2ω (half the wavelength), from light at frequency ω. Abbreviated SHG.

about.p: A material's polarization is proportional to the field for weak light, but for intense light higher-order terms appear: P = ε₀(χ⁽¹⁾E + χ⁽²⁾E² + …). The square E² of a field at frequency ω contains a component oscillating at 2ω, which radiates new light: the second harmonic. In terms of photons, two photons at ω produce one photon at 2ω. Because χ⁽²⁾ exists only in crystals lacking inversion symmetry, nonlinear optical crystals such as LiNbO₃, KTP, BBO and LBO are used. In centrosymmetric materials such as glass and silicon, it does not occur in the bulk.

For the second harmonic generated at each point in the crystal to add up, the polarization driven by the fundamental and the generated second harmonic must stay in phase through the crystal. Because of dispersion, generally n(2ω) ≠ n(ω), so on its own the SH builds up and cancels repeatedly over each coherence length (a few to tens of micrometers). Achieving Δk = 0, by birefringent phase matching, which uses birefringence to equalize the indices of waves with different polarizations, or by quasi-phase matching, which periodically reverses the crystal's spontaneous polarization (domain orientation), makes the conversion efficiency grow with the square of crystal length and with fundamental power.

A typical application is the green laser, which makes 532 nm light from a 1064 nm Nd:YAG or fiber laser. Combined with sum-frequency generation, it also yields ultraviolet light at 355 nm or 266 nm, used for fine laser machining and inspection. Its dependence on the square of power is exploited in autocorrelators that measure the width of ultrashort pulses, and in SHG microscopes, which produce signal only near the focus. Because inversion symmetry is broken at surfaces, it also serves as a spectroscopic method that selectively probes interfaces.

faq.q: How is the SHG wavelength calculated?
faq.a: The frequency doubles, so the wavelength is half the fundamental's: 532 nm for 1064 nm, 775 nm for 1550 nm. It follows from energy conservation, ħω + ħω = ħ(2ω).

faq.q: Why does SHG not occur in glass?
faq.a: Because glass is an isotropic material with inversion symmetry, its second-order susceptibility χ⁽²⁾ is zero. It does have a third-order χ⁽³⁾, so the Kerr effect and third-harmonic generation do occur.

faq.q: How can SHG efficiency be raised?
faq.a: With phase matching in place, choose a crystal with a large nonlinear coefficient, use pulses with high peak power, focus the beam, or lengthen the crystal. The efficiency rises in proportion to the fundamental power, and the SH output in proportion to its square.

位相整合.desc: In nonlinear wavelength conversion, making the wavenumber mismatch Δk = 0 so that the generated light and the driving polarization stay in phase through the crystal.

擬似位相整合.desc: A method that reverses the direction of a nonlinear crystal's spontaneous polarization (its ferroelectric domains, and with them the sign of χ⁽²⁾) every coherence length, canceling the phase slip so that conversion continues. Used in PPLN and similar materials.

光パラメトリック発振器.desc: A tunable light source that splits pump photons into signal and idler photons in a χ⁽²⁾ crystal and oscillates in a resonator. Abbreviated OPO.

光カー効果.desc: The third-order nonlinear optical effect in which the refractive index changes in proportion to light intensity, n = n₀ + n₂I. It causes self-phase modulation and self-focusing.

自己位相変調.desc: The phenomenon in which an optical pulse is phase-modulated through the Kerr effect by the time variation of its own intensity, producing a frequency chirp and broadening its spectrum. SPM.

ポッケルス効果.desc: The linear electro-optic effect, in which the refractive index of a crystal lacking inversion symmetry changes in proportion to an applied field. Used in LN modulators and electro-optic Q-switches.

光ソリトン.desc: A wave packet of light that travels through an optical fiber keeping its pulse shape, because broadening from anomalous dispersion balances the chirp from self-phase modulation.

F値.desc: The focal length divided by the entrance-pupil diameter, N = f/D. Image-plane irradiance is inversely proportional to N², so each full stop (a factor of √2 in N) halves the light.

開口絞り.desc: The stop in an optical system that sets the width of the light bundle from an on-axis object point. Its image seen from the object side is the entrance pupil, and from the image side the exit pupil.

ザイデル収差.desc: The third-order monochromatic aberrations caused by departures from the paraxial approximation: spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion.

コマ収差.desc: An aberration in which the image of an off-axis point trails like a comet because each annular zone of the pupil images at a different magnification. Proportional to the square of the aperture and to the field angle.

色消しレンズ.desc: A lens that combines a convex and a concave element of crown and flint glass with different Abbe numbers, bringing two wavelengths to the same focal position.

MTF.desc: The modulation transfer function: a measure of imaging performance that expresses, as a function of spatial frequency, how much of the contrast of a sinusoidal light-dark pattern is preserved in the image.

about.p: When an object whose brightness varies sinusoidally is imaged, the image is a sinusoid with the same period, but its contrast (Imax − Imin)/(Imax + Imin) is lower than the object's. This ratio, expressed as a function of spatial frequency (cycles per millimeter), is the MTF. In incoherent imaging the image is the convolution of the object with the point spread function (PSF), so the magnitude of the optical transfer function (OTF), the Fourier transform of the PSF, is the MTF, and its phase is the phase transfer function (PTF). It is 1 at zero frequency and normally decreases for finer patterns.

about.h: The diffraction limit and the cutoff frequency
about.p: Even for an aberration-free system with a circular aperture, diffraction makes the MTF fall smoothly with frequency, reaching zero at the cutoff frequency fc = 1/(λN) = 2NA/λ. At 0.55 µm and f/4, that is about 455 cycles/mm. Because the incoherent MTF is set by the autocorrelation of the pupil function, its cutoff is twice that for coherent illumination (NA/λ). Aberrations push the MTF below the diffraction-limited curve, especially lowering contrast at intermediate frequencies. Comparing MTFs through focus and at each off-axis image height reveals performance across the whole image plane.

about.h: MTF combined with an image sensor
about.p: The MTF of a whole camera is normally estimated as the product of the MTFs of the lens, optical low-pass filter, pixel aperture, image processing and so on. The Nyquist frequency of an image sensor with pixel pitch p is 1/(2p), about 167 cycles/mm for 3 µm pixels. If the lens MTF remains at frequencies above this, aliasing produces moiré. Lens evaluations often use the MTF at around half the Nyquist frequency, or graphs showing the MTF in two directions, radial and tangential, at each image height.

faq.q: What does MTF express?
faq.a: It expresses, for each spatial frequency, how much contrast remains in the image when stripes of different fineness are imaged. A lens whose MTF stays high up to high frequencies renders fine detail clearly.

faq.q: Is the MTF of an aberration-free lens equal to 1?
faq.a: No. Because of diffraction, the MTF falls with frequency even without aberrations, reaching zero at the cutoff frequency 1/(λN). The larger the f-number, the lower the cutoff.

faq.q: Does MTF reveal distortion?
faq.a: No. Distortion only shifts image positions and does not reduce contrast, so it does not appear in the MTF. It is evaluated separately as a distortion percentage.

被写界深度.desc: The range of object distances in front of and behind the focus distance over which image blur stays within the acceptable circle of confusion. It increases with stopping down and, at the same distance, with shorter focal length.

ストレール比.desc: The peak intensity of the point image of an aberrated system divided by that of an aberration-free, diffraction-limited system. A value of 0.8 or more is commonly taken as diffraction-limited.

比視感度.desc: A function V(λ) expressing how the brightness perceived by the human eye varies with wavelength, normalized to 1 at its peak. It peaks near 555 nm for photopic vision and near 507 nm for scotopic vision.

about.p: In bright surroundings the cones are active, and the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ) peaks at about 555 nm (yellow-green), falling off steeply toward 400 nm and 700 nm. For example, it is about 0.11 at 650 nm and about 0.04 at 450 nm. In dim surroundings the rods are active, and the peak of the scotopic function V′(λ) shifts to about 507 nm. The Purkinje effect, in which red flowers look dark and blue flowers relatively bright at dusk, comes from this shift. Both are standard functions defined by the CIE as averages over many observers.

A photometric quantity is found by multiplying the spectrum of the radiometric quantity by V(λ), integrating, and multiplying by the maximum luminous efficacy Km = 683 lm/W. For luminous flux, Φv = 683 ∫ Φe(λ) V(λ) dλ. 1 W of monochromatic light at 555 nm is 683 lm, at 532 nm (V ≈ 0.88) about 600 lm, and in the infrared or ultraviolet, where V ≈ 0, nearly 0 lm. The value 683 comes from the definition of the candela (1 cd for monochromatic light at 540 THz with a radiant intensity of 1/683 W/sr). For scotopic vision, the maximum luminous efficacy is about 1700 lm/W.

Illuminance meters and luminance meters need the spectral responsivity of their sensors matched to V(λ). A silicon photodiode's responsivity peaks around 900 nm, so correction filters made of colored glass or interference coatings are combined with it to approximate V(λ). If the correction is imperfect, errors arise when measuring white LEDs or single-color LEDs whose spectra differ from the source used for calibration (usually standard illuminant A at about 2856 K). To reduce such errors, another approach is to measure the spectrum with a spectroradiometer and then apply V(λ) by calculation.

faq.q: Why does it peak at 555 nm?
faq.a: Because the sum of the sensitivities of the L and M cones, which contribute most to brightness, is largest around yellow-green. It is also thought to be related to the strength of the solar spectrum in the visible range and to the evolution of the eye.

faq.q: How many lumens is an infrared laser?
faq.a: Outside the visible range, in the infrared or ultraviolet, V(λ) is nearly 0, so the luminous flux is nearly 0 lm. Even though the eye perceives no brightness, energy still reaches the retina and skin, so safety is assessed with radiometric quantities (W).

faq.q: What should be used to compare how bright lights are?
faq.a: To compare visible brightness, use photometric quantities such as luminous flux (lm) or illuminance (lx). Even at the same wattage, light looks dimmer the farther its wavelength is from 555 nm, and the more infrared a source contains.

光束.desc: A photometric quantity expressing the amount of light leaving a source or passing through a surface, weighted by the luminous efficiency function. Its unit is the lumen (lm); its radiometric counterpart is radiant flux (W).

光度.desc: The luminous flux per unit solid angle that a point source emits in a given direction. Its unit is the candela (cd = lm/sr). For a source uniform in all directions, it is the total luminous flux divided by 4π.

照度.desc: The luminous flux incident on a surface per unit area. Its unit is the lux (lx = lm/m²). The illuminance from a point source is inversely proportional to the square of the distance and proportional to the cosine of the angle of incidence.

輝度.desc: The brightness of a surface seen from a given direction, expressed as luminous flux per unit area per unit solid angle. Its unit is cd/m². It does not depend on viewing distance and is used for the brightness of displays.

等色関数.desc: Functions giving the amounts of three primaries needed to match the color of monochromatic light at each wavelength. Weighting a spectrum with the CIE x̄, ȳ and z̄ gives the tristimulus values XYZ.

about.p: Human color vision is determined by the responses of three types of cones, so any color can be matched by a combination of amounts of three primaries (for example, red, green and blue monochromatic lights). The color-matching functions express, as functions of wavelength, the amounts of the primaries needed to match monochromatic light at each wavelength. The three values obtained by multiplying a light's spectrum S(λ) by the color-matching functions and integrating are called the tristimulus values, and lights with the same tristimulus values look the same color even if their spectra differ (metamerism). This property is also why a display can represent many colors with only red, green and blue light.

With real red, green and blue primaries, parts of the color-matching functions become negative (because a primary must be added to the side of the monochromatic light to achieve a match). In 1931 the CIE linearly transformed these into color-matching functions x̄(λ), ȳ(λ) and z̄(λ) based on imaginary primaries that are positive everywhere. In doing so it made ȳ(λ) the same as the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ), so the tristimulus value Y is proportional to photometric quantities such as luminance. X = k∫S x̄ dλ, and Y and Z are found in the same form.

about.h: Chromaticity coordinates and the chromaticity diagram
about.p: Dividing the tristimulus values by their sum gives the chromaticity coordinates x = X/(X + Y + Z) and y = Y/(X + Y + Z), which express the properties of a color apart from its brightness. The chromaticities of monochromatic light trace the horseshoe-shaped spectral locus; a mixture of two lights lies on the line joining them, and a mixture of three lies inside their triangle. A display's color gamut is shown by this triangle. For example, the white point of standard daylight D65 is (x, y) ≈ (0.313, 0.329). Distances on the xy chromaticity diagram are not proportional to perceived color differences, so color differences are evaluated in uniform color spaces such as CIELAB.

faq.q: Do color-matching functions differ between observers?
faq.a: There are individual differences, but the CIE color-matching functions are averages over many observers and are defined as a standard observer. Because appearance changes with field size, there are two versions: the 2° field (1931) and the 10° field (1964).

faq.q: What does the tristimulus value Y represent?
faq.a: Because ȳ(λ) has the same shape as the luminous efficiency function V(λ), Y is a quantity proportional to brightness (luminance or luminous flux). The color information is carried mainly by the chromaticity coordinates x and y, which are ratios that include X and Z.

faq.q: How do RGB values differ from XYZ?
faq.a: XYZ is a device-independent color system that expresses every color with positive values. RGB spaces such as sRGB are representations based on specific three primaries and a white point, obtained from XYZ by a 3×3 matrix and a gamma conversion. Colors outside the gamut become negative or greater than 1 in RGB.

色温度.desc: The color of light expressed as the temperature (K) of the blackbody that looks that color. For sources off the blackbody locus, the temperature of the closest blackbody (correlated color temperature) is used. Higher values are bluer white.

演色評価数.desc: An index of how close the colors of objects lit by a source are to how they look under a reference light of the same color temperature. The average over eight test colors is the general color rendering index Ra, with a maximum of 100.

波長分解能.desc: A spectrometer's ability to separate close wavelengths, given by the smallest separable wavelength difference Δλ or by the ratio R = λ/Δλ (the resolving power). For a diffraction grating, the upper limit of R is mN, the product of the number of illuminated grooves and the order.

逆線分散.desc: The wavelength range spread over a unit length in a spectrometer's focal plane, dλ/dx (nm/mm). For a grating it is d cosβ/(mf); multiplying by the width of the slit image gives the bandwidth.

ブレーズド回折格子.desc: A diffraction grating whose grooves have a sawtooth cross-section, with the direction of specular reflection from the facets matched to a particular order. The diffraction efficiency of that order is high near the blaze wavelength.

フーリエ変換分光法.desc: A spectroscopic method that obtains a spectrum by Fourier transforming the interferogram recorded while varying the path difference of a Michelson interferometer. Infrared FTIR is the representative example.

about.p: When light is sent into a Michelson interferometer and the movable mirror is moved, monochromatic light of wavenumber σ = 1/λ gives an intensity that varies as cos(2πσδ) with the path difference δ. For light containing many wavenumbers, the result is an interferogram I(δ) in which the cosine waves of each component overlap, and Fourier transforming it recovers the spectrum B(σ). Two close lines produce a beat, and its period 1/Δσ gives the difference in wavenumber. The instrument widely used in infrared spectroscopy is the FTIR (Fourier transform infrared spectrometer).

The interferogram can be measured only up to a finite path difference δmax, so the spectrum is broadened by the instrument function, and the wavenumber resolution is roughly Δσ ≈ 1/δmax. Moving the mirror by x changes the path difference by 2x, so a resolution of 0.5 cm⁻¹ requires about 1 cm of travel to one side. Sampling is triggered at even intervals by the fringes of a He-Ne laser (632.8 nm) sent along the same path. With one point per fringe cycle, the Nyquist condition gives a maximum measurable wavenumber of about 7900 cm⁻¹.

Because FTIR measures all wavelengths at once, in the infrared, where detector noise dominates, the signal-to-noise ratio improves by roughly √M for M spectral points (the Fellgett advantage). Other strengths are that no narrow slit is needed so much light can be collected (the Jacquinot advantage), and that the wavenumber scale is set accurately by the laser wavelength (the Connes advantage). In the visible and ultraviolet, on the other hand, where shot noise dominates, the multiplex advantage nearly disappears, and dispersive spectrometers with array detectors are commonly used.

faq.q: What determines the resolution of an FTIR?
faq.a: It is determined by the maximum path difference δmax, roughly Δσ ≈ 1/δmax. The mirror travel is half of that. Applying apodization to suppress truncation sidelobes widens the instrument function.

faq.q: Why is it so widely used for infrared spectroscopy?
faq.a: Because infrared detectors are noisy, so the multiplex advantage of measuring all wavelengths at once counts for a lot. Even with weak infrared sources, spectra with high signal-to-noise ratio can be obtained quickly, and wavenumber accuracy can also be high.

faq.q: What is the He-Ne laser used for?
faq.a: To mark the movable mirror's position with He-Ne fringes every 632.8 nm of path difference. This allows evenly spaced sampling even if the mirror speed fluctuates, and makes the wavenumber scale accurate.

インターフェログラム.desc: A record of how the detected light intensity changes as the path difference of an interferometer is varied. Fourier transforming it gives the spectrum of the light.

自由スペクトル領域.desc: The wavelength (or frequency) range that can be used without transmission peaks or diffracted light of adjacent orders overlapping. It is λ²/(2nL) for a Fabry–Perot and about λ/m for order m of a grating.

フィネス.desc: The free spectral range of a Fabry–Perot interferometer divided by the full width at half maximum of its transmission peaks. For lossless mirrors it is π√R/(1 − R), increasing with reflectance.

about.p: The transmission peaks of a Fabry–Perot interferometer are spaced by the free spectral range (FSR), and their sharpness is expressed by the finesse F = FSR/δν (δν is the full width at half maximum). For two identical mirrors without absorption, F = π√R/(1 − R): about 30 for R = 0.90, about 103 for 0.97, and about 313 for 0.99. The quantity 4R/(1 − R)² that appears in the transmission formula T = 1/[1 + (4R/(1 − R)²) sin²(δ/2)] is a different quantity called the coefficient of finesse, so take care not to confuse them.

The resolving power of a Fabry–Perot interferometer is the product of the interference order m = 2nL/λ and the finesse, R = mF. With a mirror spacing of 5 mm, a wavelength of 500 nm and a finesse of 30, m = 20000 and R = 6×10⁵, more than an order of magnitude higher than a grating spectrometer. But the FSR, λ²/(2nL) = 0.025 nm, is narrow, so measuring a wide wavelength range requires first narrowing the range with a grating spectrometer or filter. The finesse can also be described as roughly how many resolvable peaks fit within the FSR.

Real interferometers have a lower finesse than the value set by reflectance alone. Surface irregularities of the mirrors (flatness) or a deviation from parallelism between the two shift the resonant wavelength from place to place, broadening the peaks. Obliquely incident light, beam divergence, and absorption or scattering in the mirrors do the same. As a guide, the overall finesse is found by adding the inverse squares of the finesses due to each factor, and it is set by the lowest one.
