High-finesse resonators use ultra-low-loss dielectric multilayer mirrors and reach values above 100,000.

faq.q: How is finesse calculated?
faq.a: In measurement, it is found by dividing the FSR by the full width at half maximum of a transmission peak. From the reflectance R of lossless mirrors, it can be estimated as F ≈ π√R/(1 − R). For R = 0.97 it is about 103.

faq.q: How do finesse and Q factor differ?
faq.a: Finesse is the ratio of the FSR to the peak width, and the Q factor is the ratio of the resonant frequency to the peak width. A longer resonator has a higher order, so for the same finesse the Q factor is larger, with the relation Q = mF.

faq.q: Does raising the finesse raise the resolving power without limit?
faq.a: Since the resolving power is mF, it does rise, but mirror flatness, parallelism and absorption cap the actual finesse. Also, the sharper the transmission peaks, the more strongly they are affected by fluctuations in the light frequency or the mirror spacing.

アッベ数.desc: A number expressing how small the dispersion of an optical material is, Vd = (nd − 1)/(nF − nC). The larger it is, the smaller the difference in index between wavelengths and the less chromatic aberration arises.

about.p: The Abbe number is found from the index nd at the d line (587.6 nm) and the index difference nF − nC between the F line (486.1 nm) and C line (656.3 nm), as Vd = (nd − 1)/(nF − nC). The denominator expresses the dispersion and the numerator the refracting power, so the Abbe number shows how little the colors separate relative to how strongly the material refracts. BK7-type glass is about 64, calcium fluoride about 95, and dense flint glasses around 20–30. Ve, referenced to the e line (546.1 nm), is also used.

Optical glasses are classified on a diagram (the Abbe diagram) with the index nd on the vertical axis and the Abbe number on the horizontal axis. As a guide, glasses with an Abbe number above about 50 are crown glasses and those below are flint glasses. Flint glasses contain heavy elements such as lead or titanium, giving a higher index at the cost of larger dispersion. In recent years they have been replaced by lead-free glasses for environmental reasons, but the classification works the same way.

The condition for two cemented lenses to bring two wavelengths to the same focus is φ₁/V₁ + φ₂/V₂ = 0, using the powers φ and Abbe numbers V. A positive lens of high-Abbe-number crown is combined with a negative lens of low-Abbe-number flint; the larger the difference in Abbe numbers, the weaker each lens can be, making aberration correction easier. Apochromats, which also bring a third wavelength to the same focus, use fluorite or special low-dispersion glasses with anomalous partial dispersion.

faq.q: What does a large Abbe number mean?
faq.a: The difference in index between wavelengths is small, so chromatic aberration is small even in a single lens. Calcium fluoride (about 95) and special low-dispersion glasses are used in telephoto lenses and high-performance microscope objectives to suppress color fringing.

faq.q: How is the Abbe number calculated?
faq.a: Using the indices at the d, F and C lines, Vd = (nd − 1)/(nF − nC). With nd = 1.5168 and nF − nC = 0.00806 it is about 64. Take care not to swap the numerator and denominator.

faq.q: Do higher-index glasses have lower Abbe numbers?
faq.a: As a tendency, yes: higher-index glasses have their ultraviolet absorption shifted to longer wavelengths and tend to have larger dispersion. But some materials, such as lanthanum-containing glasses, have a relatively large Abbe number despite a high index.

セルマイヤーの式.desc: An equation expressing the wavelength dependence of the refractive index as n²(λ) = 1 + Σ Bᵢλ²/(λ² − Cᵢ). Each term corresponds to an ultraviolet or infrared absorption resonance, and it represents dispersion in the transparent range accurately.

正常分散.desc: The property that the refractive index decreases as the wavelength gets longer. It is seen in the transmission range of transparent materials; inside absorption bands it reverses into anomalous dispersion.

誘電体多層膜ミラー.desc: A mirror made by alternately stacking λ/4 layers of dielectrics with different indices so that the reflections at each boundary add up. It has almost no absorption and can exceed 99.9% reflectance.

about.p: When films of high index nH and low index nL are stacked alternately, each with an optical thickness of λ₀/4, the light reflected at successive boundaries is shifted by a half wave on the round trip, and together with the phase reversal at the reflections they all add in phase. For an (HL)ᴺH structure the reflectance is R = [(1 − Y)/(1 + Y)]², Y = (nH/nL)^(2N)·nH²/ns, and each additional pair multiplies Y by (nH/nL)². Eleven layers of TiO₂ (2.35) and SiO₂ (1.45) give about 99.1%.

about.h: Width of the high-reflectance band and higher-order bands
about.p: The relative width of the band with high reflectance is Δλ/λ₀ ≈ (4/π) arcsin[(nH − nL)/(nH + nL)], set only by the index ratio; it is about 0.30 for TiO₂ and SiO₂. Adding pairs barely widens it, but increases the reflectance and sharpens the band edges. High-reflectance bands also appear at λ₀/3 and λ₀/5, where each layer is an odd multiple of λ/4, while at λ₀/2 each layer becomes a half-wave absentee layer and there is almost no reflection.

about.h: Differences from metal mirrors and uses
about.p: Aluminum and silver mirrors reflect over a wide range of wavelengths, but their absorption limits reflectance to about 90–98% and they heat up at high power. Dielectric mirrors have almost no absorption, so they are used as laser resonator mirrors and in high-finesse cavities with reflectances above 99.99%. In exchange, their reflection band is limited, and at oblique incidence the band shifts to shorter wavelengths and splits by polarization, so they are designed for a set angle and polarization.

faq.q: How does the reflectance change as pairs are added?
faq.a: Each added pair multiplies Y by (nH/nL)², and the reflectance approaches 100%. For TiO₂ and SiO₂ that is about 2.6 times per pair. The band width barely changes, however, and film stress and scattering loss grow with the number of layers.

faq.q: What happens at oblique incidence?
faq.a: The phase thickness in the films shrinks by the factor cosθ, so the reflection band shifts to shorter wavelengths. The effective indices also differ for s- and p-polarization, and the p-polarization band is narrower. Mirrors used at 45° are designed for that angle.

faq.q: Can a mirror reflect two wavelengths at once?
faq.a: A plain λ/4 stack has high-reflectance bands only at odd fractions of the design wavelength, so it cannot reflect 1064 nm and 532 nm together. This is achieved with designs whose thicknesses depart from λ/4, or by combining two stacks.

フッ化カルシウム.desc: Crystalline CaF₂. It transmits from about 0.13 µm in the vacuum ultraviolet to about 10 µm in the infrared and has low dispersion. Used in ultraviolet laser optics, infrared windows and apochromatic objectives.

レーザー損傷しきい値.desc: The fluence (J/cm²) or intensity at which laser light begins to damage an optical component or coating. It varies with wavelength, pulse width and beam size, so it is quoted together with those conditions.

応力複屈折.desc: Birefringence induced by stress in an isotropic material. The path difference is Δ = Kσd (K is the photoelastic coefficient), and residual stress in glass is expressed as path difference per cm of thickness (nm/cm).

ファイバブラッググレーティング.desc: A periodic index structure written into a fiber core that reflects only light at the Bragg wavelength λB = 2n_effΛ. Used as strain and temperature sensors and as wavelength filters.

about.h: How it reflects, and how it is written
about.p: In an FBG the core index varies slightly with period Λ, and the weak reflections from each plane add in phase at the wavelength for which the round-trip path difference 2n_effΛ is exactly one wavelength. For n_eff = 1.447 and Λ = 535.6 nm, λB ≈ 1550 nm. The reflection bandwidth is about 0.1–1 nm, and other wavelengths pass almost untouched. A common writing method changes the index of a germanium-doped core with ultraviolet laser light made to interfere through a phase mask.

Stretching the fiber lengthens the period, and the photoelastic effect slightly lowers the effective index, so the Bragg wavelength increases by ΔλB = (1 − pe)ελB. With pe ≈ 0.22 this is about 1.2 pm/µε in the 1550 nm band. A rise in temperature lengthens it by about 10 pm/K through the thermo-optic effect and thermal expansion. Since a 1 K change corresponds to about 8 µε, strain measurements subtract the temperature contribution using a strain-free reference FBG.

Because an FBG measures through changes in wavelength, it is largely immune to fluctuations in light intensity and connection losses, and it also resists electromagnetic noise. Dozens of FBGs with different Bragg wavelengths can be placed on one fiber and read out by their reflection wavelengths, measuring strain or temperature at many points simultaneously. Besides monitoring bridges, tunnels, aircraft wings and power equipment, in optical communications they also serve as wavelength filters, dispersion compensators and fiber-laser resonator mirrors.

faq.q: How sensitive is an FBG to strain?
faq.a: About 1.2 pm/µε in the 1550 nm band. A strain of 500 µε shifts the wavelength by about 0.60 nm. If the interrogator's wavelength resolution is 1 pm, strains of about 1 µε can be resolved.

faq.q: How are temperature and strain distinguished?
faq.a: The basic approach is to place nearby a reference FBG fixed so that no strain reaches it, and subtract its wavelength change as the temperature contribution. Another approach combines two kinds of FBG with different temperature sensitivities and solves the two equations for both quantities.

faq.q: How do FBGs differ from distributed sensors?
faq.a: An FBG is a point sensor that measures only where it is written (quasi-distributed when many are lined up). Raman and Brillouin distributed sensors can measure the full length of an unmodified fiber continuously, but fall short of FBGs in spatial resolution and measurement time.

分布型光ファイバセンサ.desc: A sensor that measures the backscatter in a fiber position by position, using the round-trip time, so that the whole length of the fiber acts as a continuous sensor. Raman, Brillouin and Rayleigh scattering are used for different quantities.

about.p: In distributed sensing, a light pulse is launched into the fiber and the scattered light returning is recorded over time. Light returning a time t after launch was scattered at position z = ct/(2n) (n is the group index), so information at each position is obtained in the same way as with an OTDR. The spatial resolution is set by the pulse width, about 1 m for 10 ns. A single instrument can monitor tens of km of fiber, and the sensing part needs no electricity.

about.h: Using the three kinds of scattering
about.p: In Raman scattering the anti-Stokes intensity depends strongly on temperature, so temperature is measured from its ratio to the Stokes light (DTS). In Brillouin scattering the frequency shift of about 10.8 GHz in the 1550 nm band changes with strain and temperature, so strain distributions in structures are measured (BOTDR and BOTDA). Rayleigh scattering is elastic scattering with no frequency change, and with a narrow-linewidth laser the phase of the scattered light captures vibration and sound (DAS).

Each pulse must wait until the scattered light from the previous one has returned from the far end of the fiber, so the repetition rate is limited to c/(2nL), about 2 kHz for 50 km. Because the scattered light is weak, finding temperature or strain accurately requires many averages, and measurements take longer the longer the distance and the finer the spatial resolution. Pulse width, number of averages and method are therefore chosen to suit the application.

faq.q: What distances can be measured?
faq.a: It depends on the method, but 10 to several tens of km is typical for Raman DTS, and tens of km for Brillouin methods. Fiber loss weakens the scattered light, so temperature and strain accuracy drop as the distance grows.

faq.q: Can ordinary telecom fiber be used?
faq.a: Yes. Brillouin methods and DAS can often use already-installed telecom single-mode fiber as is, while Raman DTS commonly uses multimode fiber. How the fiber is fixed changes how strain and vibration are transferred to it.

faq.q: Which is better, distributed sensing or a line of FBGs?
faq.a: FBGs suit measuring fixed points with high accuracy and speed, while distributed sensing suits finding anomalies over long sections where the location is not known in advance. The two are also used in combination.

分布型温度センサ.desc: A technique that finds the temperature at each position along a fiber from the intensity ratio of anti-Stokes to Stokes Raman scattering. Used to monitor the temperature of power cables, pipelines and wells.

ブリルアン散乱.desc: Scattering of light by sound waves in a medium. The frequency shift is 2nVa/λ, about 11 GHz in silica fiber in the 1550 nm band, and it changes with strain and temperature.

分布型音響センシング.desc: A method that detects vibration and sound along a fiber position by position, from changes in the phase of Rayleigh backscatter of narrow-linewidth light pulses. Used for seismic monitoring and intrusion detection.

FMCW.desc: A method that transmits continuous light with a linearly swept frequency and finds range from the beat frequency with the returning light and velocity from the Doppler shift. The range resolution is c/(2B).

光学式エンコーダ.desc: A sensor that measures position or rotation angle by reading a graduated grating with light. A- and B-phase signals offset by 90° determine direction, and ×4 decoding or interpolation raises the resolution.

レーザードップラー速度計.desc: A technique that measures velocities such as those of flows without contact, from the frequency v/d of light scattered by particles crossing the interference fringes formed where two laser beams cross.

空間周波数.desc: The number of times bright and dark fringes repeat per unit length, the reciprocal of the period. Expressed in cycles/mm, it is used to compare the fineness of images and the performance of lenses.

4f系.desc: An imaging system with two lenses of focal lengths f₁ and f₂ separated by f₁ + f₂, with a total length of 2f₁ + 2f₂. A Fourier plane forms between them, and the magnification is −f₂/f₁.

空間フィルタ.desc: A method of removing particular spatial-frequency components by placing a stop or pinhole in the Fourier plane. Used to clean up laser beams and to enhance edges.

フラウンホーファー回折.desc: Diffraction observed far enough from an aperture, or in the focal plane of a lens. The amplitude of the diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the aperture's amplitude distribution.

フレネル数.desc: The number NF = a²/(λL) formed from the aperture radius a, distance L and wavelength λ. When it is much smaller than 1 the diffraction is treated as Fraunhofer, and when it is around 1 as Fresnel diffraction.

タルボ効果.desc: The phenomenon in which a grating of period d illuminated with coherent light produces, without a lens, images identical to the grating at every distance 2d²/λ. Also called self-imaging.

ホログラフィ.desc: A technique that records the interference fringes between an object wave and a reference wave and reconstructs the object wavefront by diffracting the reference wave. Because it records both amplitude and phase, it gives three-dimensional images.

about.h: Recording amplitude and phase as interference fringes
about.p: Recording materials and image sensors can record only the intensity of light, and an ordinary photograph loses the phase information. In holography, a coherent reference wave R, split from the same source, is superposed on the object wave O scattered by the object, and the intensity |O + R|² is recorded. The OR* and O*R terms in it form interference fringes, writing the phase of the object wave into the positions of the fringes and its amplitude into their contrast. Recording requires a source coherence length longer than the optical path difference between the two waves, and enough stability that the fringes do not move during exposure.

When the recorded hologram is illuminated with the reference wave R, diffraction by the fringes produces a component of the transmitted light proportional to the object wave O, reproducing the wavefront of the light that came from the original object. That is why a three-dimensional image with depth, whose appearance changes as the viewing position changes, is seen. At the same time a phase-reversed conjugate image (twin image) and zeroth-order light also appear. In Gabor's in-line type these overlapped on the same axis, but Leith and Upatnieks, with the off-axis type in which the reference wave enters at an angle, made it possible to separate and observe the images.

In a volume hologram recorded in a thick material, the fringes form layers inside the material, and only wavelengths and angles satisfying the Bragg condition are strongly diffracted. Reflection volume holograms can reconstruct images with little color smearing even under white light. The holograms most widely used against counterfeiting on banknotes and cards, however, are embossed holograms, whose fringes are mass-produced as surface relief by stamping. In digital holography, which records the hologram with an image sensor and reconstructs it by computing diffraction, the phase distribution of the object wave is obtained as numbers, so it is used to measure the thickness of transparent cells and the shape of surfaces. Because the pixels are large, the reference angle is limited to a few degrees or less.

faq.q: How does a hologram differ from an ordinary photograph?
faq.a: A photograph records only the intensity distribution of light imaged by a lens. A hologram records both the amplitude and phase of light as interference fringes with a reference wave, so on reconstruction the very wavefront from the object is reproduced, giving a three-dimensional image whose appearance changes with viewing direction.

faq.q: Why is a laser needed to record a hologram?
faq.a: For the object and reference waves to form stable interference fringes, a coherence length longer than the optical path difference is needed. The coherence length of white light is only on the order of µm, so the fringes quickly become invisible. Reflection volume holograms can be reconstructed with white light, but recording requires coherent light.

faq.q: How fine are the interference fringes?
faq.a: When two waves cross at an angle θ, the spacing is λ/(2 sin(θ/2)). At a wavelength of 633 nm and 30° it is about 1.22 µm (about 820 cycles/mm), so recording uses dedicated high-resolution plates or photopolymers, and vibration is suppressed.

計算機ホログラム.desc: A hologram whose fringe or phase distribution, designed to produce a desired wavefront, is created by computation. Realized with spatial light modulators or microfabrication, and used for beam shaping and optical tweezers.

ケーラー照明.desc: An illumination method that images the light source onto the condenser aperture diaphragm and the field diaphragm onto the specimen plane. It lights the field evenly regardless of source unevenness and lets the illumination NA be adjusted.

暗視野照明.desc: A method that illuminates at angles larger than the objective's NA so that direct light does not enter the objective, forming the image only from light scattered or diffracted by the specimen. The background is dark and fine particles appear to glow.

位相差顕微鏡.desc: A microscope that shifts the phase of the direct light by about λ/4 with a phase plate and makes it interfere with the diffracted light, turning phase differences in transparent specimens into brightness differences. Devised by Zernike.

微分干渉顕微鏡.desc: A microscope that passes two beams of orthogonal polarization, shifted slightly sideways, through the specimen and shows the gradient of optical path difference as shaded brightness. Also called DIC.

ストークスシフト.desc: The shift of the fluorescence wavelength to longer than the excitation wavelength. It arises because an excited molecule loses energy through vibrational relaxation before emitting, and it allows filters to separate the excitation light from the fluorescence.

共焦点顕微鏡.desc: A microscope that scans the specimen with light focused to a point and blocks light from outside the focal plane with a pinhole at a position conjugate to the focus, giving images of a thin layer along the optical axis (optical sections).

about.h: Selecting the focal plane with a pinhole
about.p: In a confocal microscope, the objective focuses laser light to a single point in the specimen, and the fluorescence or reflected light from there is collected by the same objective and detected through a pinhole placed at a position conjugate to the focus. Light from the focal plane is focused onto the pinhole and passes through, but light from above or below the focal plane is spread out at the pinhole and is mostly blocked. Even in thick specimens there is therefore little blur from outside the focal plane, and optical sections showing only a thin layer along the optical axis are obtained. Stacking sections while shifting the focus little by little lets you assemble a three-dimensional image.

The pinhole diameter is expressed in Airy units, with 1 Airy unit equal to the diameter of the Airy disk at the detection plane (1.22λ/NA at the specimen plane multiplied by the magnification). At around 1 Airy unit, the pinhole removes out-of-focus light well while passing most of the light from the focus. Making it smaller still improves the lateral resolution by up to about 1.4 times, because the image is set by the product of the illumination and detection point images, but the light passing through drops sharply and the signal-to-noise ratio falls. The axial resolution is several times worse than the lateral and is inversely proportional to the square of NA, so higher-NA objectives give thinner sections.

about.h: Scanning methods and differences from other techniques
about.p: The image is built by arranging point-by-point signals through scanning, most commonly by sweeping the beam with galvanometer mirrors. The spinning-disk type, using a rotating disk with many pinholes (a Nipkow disk), scans many points at once and images quickly, so it suits observing fast movements in living cells. A two-photon excitation microscope obtains optical sections without a pinhole by not emitting fluorescence outside the focus. The difference is that confocal selects the focal plane on the detection side and two-photon on the excitation side, and in deep, strongly scattering tissue two-photon has the advantage.

faq.q: How does a confocal microscope differ from an ordinary fluorescence microscope?
faq.a: An ordinary (widefield) fluorescence microscope illuminates the whole field and records out-of-focus fluorescence as it is, so in thick specimens the blur piles up. A confocal microscope illuminates and scans with a point and blocks light from outside the focal plane with a pinhole, giving sharp images of only a thin layer.

faq.q: How large should the pinhole be?
faq.a: About 1 Airy unit is commonly used. With 63× magnification, NA 1.4 and a fluorescence wavelength of 520 nm it is about 28.5 µm. Making it smaller thins the section but darkens the image; making it larger brightens it at the cost of mixing in out-of-focus light.

faq.q: Why is the depth resolution worse than the lateral resolution?
faq.a: Because the objective collects light only over a limited range of angles from one side of the specimen, the range of spatial frequencies it can capture along the optical axis is narrower than laterally. The axial resolution is inversely proportional to the square of NA, so it improves as higher-NA objectives are used.

二光子励起顕微鏡.desc: A microscope that excites fluorescence through simultaneous absorption of two photons. Because absorption is proportional to the square of the intensity, only the focus is excited, and near-infrared light allows deep observation in living tissue.

STED顕微鏡.desc: A super-resolution microscope that switches off fluorescence around the excited spot by stimulated emission with a doughnut-shaped beam, making the emitting region narrower than the diffraction limit.

外部量子効率.desc: In an LED or similar device, the number of photons leaving the device per injected electron. It is the product of the injection efficiency, internal quantum efficiency and light-extraction efficiency.

about.p: Driving an LED with current I injects I/q electrons per second. The external quantum efficiency (EQE) is the fraction of these that leave the device as photons, found from the optical output P and wavelength λ as EQE = (Pλ/hc)/(I/q). With wavelength in nm, current in A and optical output in W, EQE ≈ Pλ/(1240 I). It differs from the wall-plug efficiency, a power ratio (optical output / electrical input); because the drive voltage exceeds the photon energy, the wall-plug efficiency is smaller than the external quantum efficiency by that margin.

The external quantum efficiency is the product of the injection efficiency with which electrons and holes reach the active layer, the internal quantum efficiency (the fraction of recombinations in the active layer that produce photons), and the light-extraction efficiency (the fraction of generated photons that escape). InGaN blue LEDs reach high internal quantum efficiencies, and the remaining challenge is extraction. From a crystal with an index of about 2.5, only about 4% of the light can leave through each flat face into air, so surface roughening, patterned substrates, resin encapsulation and reflective electrodes are combined to raise extraction.

The external quantum efficiency changes with current: at low current, defect-assisted nonradiative recombination is relatively large, and raising the current raises the efficiency. Raising the current density further increases Auger recombination and carrier leakage, and the efficiency falls, which is called efficiency droop. A hotter active layer also lowers the efficiency through more nonradiative recombination, so for lighting LEDs, enlarging the chip to lower the current density and good thermal design are keys to maintaining efficiency. The same definition of external quantum efficiency is used for OLEDs.

faq.q: What is the difference between external quantum efficiency and luminous efficacy (lm/W)?
faq.a: External quantum efficiency is the ratio of numbers of photons and electrons, a physical efficiency independent of the color of light. Luminous efficacy is the luminous flux (lm) per watt of power, weighted by the eye's sensitivity, so for the same external quantum efficiency it is larger for light closer to the green where the eye is most sensitive.

faq.q: How is the optical output found from the external quantum efficiency?
faq.a: The optical output is P = EQE × (I/q) × (hc/λ). For example, at 350 mA, 450 nm and an external quantum efficiency of 52%, using a photon energy of about 2.76 eV gives about 0.5 W.

faq.q: How is the internal quantum efficiency measured?
faq.a: It is hard to measure directly, so it is estimated by taking the ratio of emission intensity at room temperature to that at low temperature, where nonradiative recombination is assumed to stop, or by analyzing the current-output relation with a recombination model. The light-extraction efficiency is estimated by calculations such as ray tracing.

光取り出し効率.desc: The fraction of photons generated in the active layer that can escape the device. Inside a high-index semiconductor, light is trapped by total internal reflection, so it is raised by surface roughening and similar means.

効率ドループ.desc: The fall in an LED's external quantum efficiency at high currents after it peaks at some current. Auger recombination and carrier leakage are considered the main causes.

白色LED.desc: An LED that converts part of a blue LED's light to yellow or other colors with a phosphor and mixes them into white. Adding a red phosphor raises color rendering but tends to lower luminous efficacy.

有機EL.desc: A device that emits light when current flows through thin films of organic material. Its pixels emit by themselves, so displays can show deep black, and phosphorescent materials that also emit from triplets raise the efficiency.

液晶ディスプレイ.desc: A display that passes or blocks backlight pixel by pixel with two polarizers and a liquid crystal whose molecular orientation changes with voltage.

色域.desc: The range of colors a display or similar device can reproduce. On a chromaticity diagram it is the inside of the triangle with the three primaries' chromaticities as vertices; standards include sRGB and BT.2020.

about.p: A display makes colors by varying the intensities of red, green and blue primaries. The chromaticity of additively mixed light is a weighted average of the primaries' chromaticities, so reproducible colors are limited to the inside of the triangle on the xy chromaticity diagram whose vertices are the three primaries. This is the color gamut. Monochromatic light lies on the horseshoe-shaped spectral locus, and no colors exist outside it, so no choice of three primaries can reproduce every visible color. The triangle is drawn in chromaticity, which is independent of brightness, so high luminance has nothing to do with the width of the gamut.

about.h: Gamut standards and how to compare them
about.p: Standards such as sRGB for computers and the web, Adobe RGB for photography and printing, DCI-P3 for cinema and BT.2020 for ultra-high-definition television each define primary chromaticities and a white point. The BT.2020 primaries are monochromatic light on the spectral locus, giving a much larger triangle than sRGB. A display's gamut is expressed as its area ratio to a standard's triangle or as the fraction of the standard's triangle it covers (coverage). Distances on the xy diagram are not proportional to perceived color differences, so the u′v′ diagram is also used, and you need to check which diagram a figure was calculated on.

about.h: Technologies for wider gamut, and color management
about.p: The narrower the primaries' spectra, the closer their chromaticities move to the spectral locus and the wider the gamut. With white-LED backlights and color filters the primaries tend to be broad, so color conversion with quantum dots or narrow-band phosphors, or microcavities that narrow OLED emission, are used. Even on a wide-gamut display, however, sRGB images are shown oversaturated unless the values are converted from the image's color space to the display's. The color management of the operating system and applications performs this conversion.

faq.q: Is a wider color gamut always a better display?
faq.a: It is an advantage in that more colors can be shown, but seeing correct colors requires color management. Without it, sRGB images look too vivid and unnatural, so being able to switch to an sRGB mode for some uses also matters.

faq.q: What does "72% NTSC" mean?
faq.a: It usually expresses the area ratio of a display's triangle to the triangle of primaries of NTSC, an old television standard. The sRGB triangle has about 71% of the NTSC area on the xy diagram, so "72% NTSC" indicates a gamut roughly the size of sRGB.

faq.q: How are colors outside the gamut shown?
faq.a: A display cannot produce colors outside its triangle, so color management replaces them with nearby colors inside it (gamut mapping). Methods include reducing only saturation and compressing everything to keep the relations between colors, chosen according to the purpose.

量子ドット.desc: A semiconductor nanoparticle a few nm in size. Its emission wavelength changes with size and its spectrum is narrow, so it is used for color conversion that widens display color gamut.

CMOSイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor with an amplifying transistor in each pixel, read out by selecting rows. Everything up to AD conversion can be integrated on the same chip, making it fast and low in power.

about.p: A typical four-transistor pixel consists of a photodiode that converts light to electrons and stores them, a transfer gate that moves the charge to the floating diffusion, a reset transistor that initializes the floating diffusion, an amplifying (source-follower) transistor that converts charge to voltage, and a row-select transistor. The floating diffusion's capacitance C sets the voltage per electron q/C (conversion gain), a few tens of µV per electron for a few fF. Correlated double sampling, which takes the difference between the voltage just after reset and after charge transfer, cancels the kTC noise that changes at every reset and holds the read noise to a few electrons or less.

about.h: Readout and the difference from CCDs
about.p: A CMOS image sensor selects one row at a time, amplifies the voltages of that row's pixels in parallel with per-column circuits, AD-converts them, and outputs digital values. It does not transfer charge over long distances as a CCD does, so no high transfer voltages are needed, power is low and readout is fast. Timing control, AD conversion and even image-processing circuits can be integrated in the same semiconductor process. Early devices suffered from larger pixel-to-pixel variation and noise than CCDs, but pinned photodiodes and correlated double sampling overcame this, and they are now used in most cameras.

As pixels shrink, the wiring above the photodiode blocks light, so backside-illuminated sensors, which thin the wafer and let light in from the back, are widely used. Stacked sensors go further, making the pixel layer and the signal-processing layer on separate wafers and bonding them, so the pixel area can be devoted to receiving light and the circuits can use a high-speed logic process. A rolling shutter that exposes rows in sequence is the basic mode, but there are also global-shutter sensors with a storage element in each pixel to hold the charge temporarily, used for imaging and measuring fast-moving objects.

faq.q: Which gives better image quality, a CMOS image sensor or a CCD?
faq.a: Today CMOS image sensors match or exceed CCDs in most uses, with read noise down to about 1 to 2 electrons. CCDs were used in some scientific measurements that benefit from low pixel-to-pixel variation and binning in the charge domain, but they are being replaced by scientific CMOS image sensors.

faq.q: What are the drawbacks of a small pixel pitch?
faq.a: Each pixel receives fewer photons, so the shot-noise-limited S/N falls, and the full-well capacity also shrinks, tending to narrow the dynamic range. Diffraction blur also easily exceeds the pixel size, so detail is lost at large f-numbers.

faq.q: What is conversion gain?
faq.a: It is the voltage in µV that one electron produces in the pixel, q/C for a floating-diffusion capacitance C. A larger value makes later-stage noise less significant but reduces the number of electrons that fit in the same voltage range.

CCDイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor that transfers each pixel's charge step by step by switching electrode voltages and converts it to voltage with a few output amplifiers. Pixel-to-pixel variation is small.

フルウェル容量.desc: The maximum number of electrons a pixel can store. Beyond it the pixel saturates; it sets the bright end of the dynamic range and the maximum S/N obtainable (its square root).

読み出し雑音.desc: Noise added when a pixel's charge is converted to voltage and read out, expressed as an rms number of electrons. It sets the S/N in dark scenes and the dark end of the dynamic range.

ダイナミックレンジ.desc: The ratio of the largest signal a measurement or recording can handle to the smallest, set by noise. For image sensors, the ratio of full-well capacity to read noise is expressed in dB or stops.

about.h: The ratio of full-well capacity to read noise
about.p: An image sensor's pixel cannot hold more electrons than its full-well capacity, and brighter areas saturate to white. On the dark side, read noise and dark-current noise exist even without light, and smaller signals are buried in them. Dynamic range is the ratio of these two; for example, with a full-well capacity of 20000 electrons and read noise of 4 electrons, the ratio is 5000. Treating electron counts as amplitudes and expressing this in 20 log₁₀ gives about 74 dB, or about 12.3 stops in factors of two. Camera specifications sometimes give values that include the AD conversion bit depth and image processing.

Dynamic range is the range of brightness one image can handle, a different quantity from S/N, which describes image quality at a given brightness. Because of photon shot noise, even filling the pixel to full well gives an S/N of only √20000 ≈ 141 (about 43 dB). In other words, a sensor with 74 dB of dynamic range does not give a pixel an S/N of 74 dB. S/N in dark areas is set by the read noise and in bright areas by the amount of light, so a high dynamic range needs both a large full-well capacity and a small read noise.

Satisfying both in one pixel is difficult, so various techniques exist: dual gain, which switches the floating-diffusion capacitance to read with high conversion gain in dark scenes and low conversion gain in bright ones; HDR shooting, which combines several images with different exposure times; and pixels with an extra capacitance into which overflowing charge is stored separately. Raising the ISO setting (raising the gain) reduces the number of electrons that reaches the AD converter's maximum, so the dynamic range narrows. For high-contrast subjects such as backlit scenes, shooting at low ISO is advantageous.

faq.q: Is dynamic range expressed in dB or in stops?
faq.a: Sensor specifications often use dB with 20 log₁₀, and photography uses stops (EV) with log₂. One stop corresponds to about 6.02 dB, so 74 dB is about 12.3 stops.

faq.q: What is the dynamic range of the human eye?
faq.a: Even when viewing a single scene it is said to handle roughly 10 stops or more, and including adaptation to brightness it covers a far wider range, from starlight to daylight. The value changes greatly depending on whether adaptation is included, so the conditions need care when comparing.

faq.q: Does increasing the AD conversion bit depth widen the dynamic range?
faq.a: The sensor's own dynamic range is set by the full-well capacity and read noise and does not widen with more bits. With too few bits, however, quantization noise loses tonal gradation in the shadows, so a bit depth matching the sensor's performance is needed.

ベイヤー配列.desc: A color filter array with two green, one red and one blue filter in each 2×2 block of pixels. Each pixel measures one color only, and the others are interpolated from surrounding pixels (demosaicing).

裏面照射型.desc: An image sensor structure in which light enters from the side opposite the wiring layers (the back of the wafer). Light is not blocked by wiring, so even small pixels keep their sensitivity.

ローリングシャッタ.desc: An electronic shutter scheme that exposes and reads out each row at a slightly shifted time. Fast-moving subjects are recorded distorted. The scheme that exposes all pixels at once is the global shutter.

波長分割多重.desc: A multiplexing method that places a separate signal on light at each of several frequencies and sends them through one fiber at the same time. Capacity grows in proportion to the number of wavelengths.

光信号対雑音比.desc: The ratio of the optical signal power to the optical noise power within a defined bandwidth (usually 0.1 nm). Set mainly by amplifier ASE noise, it is used as a measure of transmission quality.

分散補償ファイバ.desc: Fiber with large chromatic dispersion of the opposite sign to the transmission fiber. It is inserted along the link or at the receiver to cancel accumulated dispersion.

利得平坦化フィルタ.desc: An optical filter with a loss spectrum that cancels the wavelength dependence of EDFA gain. It is used to equalize channel powers in cascaded amplification.

四光波混合.desc: A third-order nonlinear optical effect in which light at f_i + f_j − f_k is generated from light at three frequencies. It becomes strong when dispersion is small and causes crosstalk in WDM.

パワーバジェット.desc: The loss budget that allocates the difference between transmitter output and receiver sensitivity to fiber and connection losses and a margin. It is used to estimate the maximum transmission distance of an optical link.

直交振幅変調.desc: A modulation format that places information on the amplitudes of both the in-phase and quadrature components of the carrier. 16QAM uses 16 constellation points and carries 4 bits per symbol.

コヒーレント受信.desc: A reception method that interferes the received signal with a local oscillator to measure the amplitude and phase of the field. It allows demodulation of multilevel formats and digital compensation of chromatic dispersion.

about.h: Measuring phase through interference with a local oscillator
about.p: A photodetector's current is proportional to optical intensity, so intensity-modulated signals can be received by direct detection, but information carried in the phase is lost. Coherent detection superimposes the signal with laser light at a nearby frequency (the local oscillator, LO) before detection. An interference term between the signal and the LO appears in the intensity, and its size and sign reflect the signal amplitude and phase. A stronger LO makes the interference term larger, which also raises sensitivity relative to the receiver's thermal noise. Taking two sets of interference with the phase shifted by 0 and π/2 in a 90° hybrid yields the in-phase component I and the quadrature component Q of the field.

about.h: Configuration of a digital coherent receiver
about.p: A practical receiver splits the signal into two polarizations with a polarization beam splitter, mixes each with the LO in a 90° hybrid, and detects I and Q with four balanced photodetector pairs. A balanced detector takes the difference of two photodetectors, cancelling the LO's own intensity component and its fluctuations. The four resulting electrical signals are digitized by high-speed A/D converters, and signal processing estimates and removes the frequency offset and phase fluctuations relative to the LO. Optical phase locking of the LO to the signal is therefore unnecessary, and the intradyne scheme, which uses an independently running narrow-linewidth laser as the LO, is used.

about.h: What digital signal processing can do
about.p: Because the field is obtained as digital values, linear impairments from the link can be removed by computation. Chromatic dispersion is a frequency-dependent phase change, so a filter with the inverse characteristic can compensate even thousands of km of it, making dispersion-compensating fiber unnecessary. Even when polarization rotates in the fiber and the signals on the two polarizations mix, adaptive filters can separate them, compensating polarization-mode dispersion at the same time. This made it possible to combine polarization multiplexing with multilevel formats such as QPSK and 16QAM to send hundreds of Gb/s per wavelength. Nonlinear degradation from the Kerr effect, on the other hand, is not as easy to remove as linear impairments.

faq.q: How does it differ from direct detection?
faq.a: Direct detection measures only optical intensity, so it is used with intensity modulation (NRZ or PAM4) and is simple and inexpensive. Coherent detection measures the field amplitude and phase through interference with a local oscillator, so it can demodulate multilevel formats that use phase and polarization and can compensate dispersion digitally, but the receiver is more complex and consumes more power.

faq.q: Must the local oscillator frequency match the signal exactly?
faq.a: Not in digital coherent detection. Frequency offsets up to the GHz range and phase fluctuations can be estimated and removed by digital signal processing. A wide laser linewidth makes phase estimation harder, however, so higher-order modulation needs narrower-linewidth lasers.

faq.q: Where is it used?
faq.a: Mainly in transmission over tens to thousands of km: long-haul backbone links, submarine cables and links between data centers. Over short distances such as inside a data center, low-cost, low-power direct detection is mostly used.

時間帯域幅積.desc: The product ΔνΔt of a pulse's duration and spectral width. Its lower limit depends on the pulse shape: 0.441 for a Gaussian and 0.315 for sech². Equality holds when there is no chirp.

チャープ.desc: A change in the instantaneous frequency within a pulse over time. When the frequency rises with time it is called up-chirp. It arises from dispersion and self-phase modulation.

群遅延分散.desc: The rate at which group delay changes with angular frequency, d²φ/dω² (in fs²). When positive, long wavelengths travel ahead and the pulse up-chirps and broadens.

可飽和吸収体.desc: A material or device whose absorption decreases (saturates) as light gets stronger. In a cavity, stronger peaks see lower loss, so it is used for passive mode locking and passive Q-switching.

チャープパルス増幅.desc: An amplification method for high-intensity ultrashort pulses that stretches the pulse with dispersion to lower its peak power, amplifies it, and finally compresses it back to the original short pulse.

光周波数コム.desc: Light with many sharp, equally spaced spectral lines. The frequency of each line is fₙ = nf_rep + f_ceo; combs are obtained from mode-locked lasers and similar sources.

about.h: A pulse train and a comb of frequencies
about.p: A mode-locked laser keeps emitting pulses of the same shape every round-trip time T = 1/f_rep. The spectrum of a periodic signal consists of lines spaced by the inverse of the period, so the spectrum of the pulse train is tens of thousands to millions of sharp lines spaced by f_rep, in other words a comb. The shorter the pulses, the wider the range covered by the lines, and the longer and more stably the pulse train continues, the narrower each line becomes. The lines are not exactly at integer multiples of f_rep: all of them are shifted by a common offset frequency f_ceo, and the frequency of the nth line is fₙ = nf_rep + f_ceo.

about.h: The offset frequency and how it is measured
about.p: f_ceo arises because cavity dispersion makes the phase velocity of the carrier differ from the group velocity of the envelope, so the relative phase between carrier and envelope (the carrier-envelope phase) slips by Δφ from pulse to pulse; f_ceo = (Δφ/2π) f_rep. f_rep can be measured directly as a microwave frequency by detecting the pulse train, but f_ceo cannot. Instead the spectrum is broadened to at least an octave, and f-2f self-referencing, which doubles a line on the low-frequency side and beats it with a line on the high-frequency side, gives 2fₙ − f₂ₙ = f_ceo. Locking the two frequencies to a microwave reference fixes the frequency of every line.

about.h: Uses as a ruler for optical frequency
about.p: A comb with f_rep and f_ceo stabilized becomes a frequency ruler that links microwave and optical frequencies in a single step. The frequency of an unknown laser is found simply by measuring its beat with a nearby comb line and adding it to or subtracting it from fₙ, which made the large frequency chains of the past unnecessary. Conversely, locking a comb to the stable optical frequency of an optical clock transfers that stability to the microwave domain. Other uses include dual-comb spectroscopy, which measures broadband spectra quickly with two combs whose repetition rates differ slightly, wavelength calibration of astronomical spectrographs, and precise distance measurement.

faq.q: What sets the spacing of the comb lines?
faq.a: In a mode-locked laser it is the repetition rate f_rep, the inverse of the cavity round-trip time. In fiber lasers it is typically tens of MHz to 1 GHz, while microcombs generated in tiny optical resonators reach tens of GHz to THz.

faq.q: Why is f_ceo not zero?
faq.a: Inside the cavity the phase velocity of the carrier differs from the group velocity of the pulse envelope, so each time a pulse is emitted the position of the carrier crests relative to the envelope peak has shifted. This slip advancing at a constant rate corresponds to shifting the frequency of every line by the same amount.

faq.q: What can a frequency comb tell us?
faq.a: It lets optical frequencies themselves be counted with the same accuracy as a microwave frequency standard. It is therefore used to compare optical clocks, measure absolute laser frequencies, and for spectroscopy and precise distance measurement.

キャリア・エンベロープ位相.desc: The phase of the carrier relative to the peak of the pulse envelope. In pulses only a few cycles long it determines the shape of the electric field, and its pulse-to-pulse slip becomes the f_ceo of a frequency comb.

強度自己相関.desc: A method that splits a pulse in two with a delay and measures the strength of the second harmonic generated by their overlap as a function of delay. The result is converted to a pulse duration by assuming a pulse shape.

2次の相関関数.desc: The temporal correlation of light intensity, g⁽²⁾(τ) = ⟨I(t)I(t + τ)⟩/⟨I⟩². At τ = 0 it is 1 for laser light, 2 for thermal light and below 1 for a single-photon source.

about.h: Measuring intensity fluctuations by coincidence counting
about.p: The second-order correlation function g⁽²⁾(τ) = ⟨I(t)I(t + τ)⟩/⟨I⟩² is the correlation between the light intensity at one time and at a time τ later, divided by the square of the mean intensity. In terms of photons, it tells how many times more likely it is, compared with completely random arrivals, to detect a second photon a time τ after detecting the first. A single detector cannot measure short τ because of its dead time, so an HBT arrangement is used that splits the light with a beam splitter and counts coincidences between 2 detectors, normalizing by the expected number of accidental coincidences R₁R₂ΔtT.

Stabilized laser light (a coherent state) does not fluctuate in intensity, photons arrive at random, and g⁽²⁾ = 1 for every τ. Thermal light fluctuates in intensity over about the coherence time, and photons arrive in bunches during bright moments, so g⁽²⁾(0) = 2, returning to 1 when τ is longer than the coherence time (bunching). A single atom or quantum dot cannot emit another photon until it is re-excited after emitting one, so g⁽²⁾(0) < 1, approaching 1 as τ grows (antibunching).

For classical electromagnetic intensities the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality guarantees g⁽²⁾(0) ≥ 1, so g⁽²⁾(0) < 1 is direct evidence of the quantum nature of light. A photon-number state |n⟩ has g⁽²⁾(0) = 1 − 1/n, and light from N independent single-photon sources has 1 − 1/N, so a value below 0.5 indicates that the light comes mainly from a single emitter. In characterizing single-photon sources, g⁽²⁾(0) is a measure of how rarely 2 or more photons are mixed in, and it is a basic performance figure for sources used in quantum key distribution and photonic quantum computing.

faq.q: Why isn't g⁽²⁾(0) measured with a single detector?
faq.a: After counting a photon, a single-photon detector cannot count again for a while (its dead time), so it cannot distinguish 2 photons that arrive almost together. Splitting the light onto 2 detectors lets coincidences near zero delay be measured regardless of either detector's dead time.

faq.q: Why is g⁽²⁾(0) = 2 sometimes not observed even for thermal light?
faq.a: The bunching of thermal light is about as wide as its coherence time, which for white light is extremely short, on the order of fs, so it is smeared out by the detectors' timing resolution. A narrowband filter is used to lengthen the coherence time, or detectors with higher timing resolution are used.

faq.q: Is a smaller g⁽²⁾(0) always a better single-photon source?
faq.a: g⁽²⁾(0) expresses how rarely 2 or more photons are emitted at once, and the closer it is to 0, the purer the single photons. However, the efficiency with which photons can be extracted (brightness) and the indistinguishability of the photons (the depth of the Hong–Ou–Mandel dip) must be evaluated separately.

HBT干渉計.desc: An arrangement that splits light with a beam splitter and measures coincidences between 2 detectors as a function of delay. It determines g⁽²⁾(τ) to study photon bunching and antibunching.

スクイーズド光.desc: Light in which the fluctuation of one quadrature of the field is reduced below that of the vacuum, while the other increases. It is used for measurements with noise below shot noise.

自発的パラメトリック下方変換.desc: A process in a χ⁽²⁾ crystal in which one pump photon splits into 2 photons while conserving energy and momentum. It is used as a source of photon pairs and entangled photon pairs.

量子もつれ.desc: Correlation among several particles whose joint state cannot be written as a product of individual states. In a polarization-entangled photon pair, neither photon's polarization is defined, yet the measurement results are strongly correlated.

単一光子アバランシェダイオード.desc: A photodiode biased above breakdown (Geiger mode) that detects a single photon by triggering an avalanche. It has a dead time and afterpulsing.

超伝導ナノワイヤ単一光子検出器.desc: A detector that uses a superconducting wire, cooled to cryogenic temperature, that turns locally normal when it absorbs a photon. It has high efficiency even in the near infrared, with low dark counts and small timing jitter.

量子鍵配送.desc: A method of sharing a cryptographic key encoded in quantum states such as those of photons. Measuring the states to eavesdrop introduces errors, so the error rate reveals whether eavesdropping occurred. BB84 is the best-known protocol.

about.p: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a way for a sender and receiver to share random numbers for use as a cryptographic key by encoding them in quantum states such as the polarization or phase of photons. An unknown quantum state cannot be copied perfectly (the no-cloning theorem), and measuring to distinguish states that are not mutually orthogonal disturbs them. So if an eavesdropper measures photons along the way, errors increase in the receiver's results. The sender and receiver reveal part of the key to check the error rate, estimate how much information may have leaked, and decide whether the key can be used.

In the representative BB84 protocol, the sender picks one of 2 bases, 0°/90° or 45°/135°, at random and sends a polarized photon, and the receiver measures in a randomly chosen basis. Afterwards only the bases are compared over a public channel, and the roughly half of the bits where they agree are kept (sifting). If an eavesdropper measures every photon in a random basis and resends it, the kept bits have an error rate of 25%. If the error rate is below the tolerable value, error correction is followed by privacy amplification, which shortens the key to cancel the leaked information, to produce the final key.

Many systems use attenuated laser pulses instead of ideal single-photon sources. The photon number follows a Poisson distribution, and a photon-number-splitting attack, in which an eavesdropper takes 1 photon from the occasional pulse containing 2 or more, is possible, so the decoy-state method, which mixes in pulses of different intensities, is used as a countermeasure. The photons that arrive fall off exponentially with distance because of fiber loss, and quantum states cannot be boosted with ordinary optical amplifiers, so the distance spanned by a single link is limited. Longer distances are being considered with trusted relay nodes or quantum repeaters that use entanglement.

faq.q: Does quantum key distribution send the ciphertext itself?
faq.a: Only the random numbers that become the key are sent; the ciphertext goes over an ordinary channel. The shared key is used as a one-time pad or as the key of a symmetric cipher, and the quantum properties are used to confirm that the key has not been stolen.

faq.q: Can it prevent eavesdropping completely?
faq.a: It does not stop eavesdropping itself; its feature is that eavesdropping shows up as an increased error rate. If the error rate is high the key is discarded, and if it is acceptable, privacy amplification makes the eavesdropper's information small enough. Security assumes the equipment behaves as the theoretical model says, so countermeasures against implementation weaknesses are also needed.

faq.q: Why can't optical amplifiers extend the distance?
faq.a: Multiplying photons with an optical amplifier amounts to copying the incoming quantum state, which the no-cloning theorem forbids from being done exactly, and spontaneous-emission noise is added as well. Extending the distance requires a trusted relay that receives and resends the key at a node, or a quantum repeater that uses entanglement.

光起電力効果.desc: The appearance of a voltage across the terminals when electrons and holes generated by light are separated by a junction's built-in field. It delivers power without an external supply and underlies solar cells.

開放電圧.desc: The voltage of a solar cell with its terminals open. It is where photocurrent and recombination current balance, given roughly by (kT/q) ln(J_sc/J₀); qV_oc is smaller than the bandgap.

短絡電流.desc: The current that flows when a solar cell's terminals are shorted. The short-circuit current density J_sc per unit area is set by the number of incident photons and the external quantum efficiency.

曲線因子.desc: The maximum power divided by the product of open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current, FF. It expresses how square the I-V curve is and is reduced by series resistance, shunt resistance and recombination.

about.h: How square the I-V curve is
about.p: On a solar cell's I-V curve, the power is 0 at both the short-circuit point (zero voltage, current I_sc) and the open-circuit point (zero current, voltage V_oc), and between them lies the maximum power point (V_mp, I_mp), where the product of current and voltage is largest. The fill factor is FF = V_mpI_mp/(V_ocI_sc), the ratio of the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside the curve to that of the rectangle formed by I_sc and V_oc. The more square the curve, the closer it gets to 1, but because of the exponential diode characteristic even an ideal cell never reaches 1.

For a diode with ideality factor n, the approximation FF ≈ (v_oc − ln(v_oc + 0.72))/(v_oc + 1) is widely used, with the normalized open-circuit voltage v_oc = V_oc/(nkT/q). The higher the open-circuit voltage, the higher FF; with V_oc = 0.7 V, n = 1 and 300 K, v_oc ≈ 27 and FF is about 0.85. Cells with higher open-circuit voltages, such as GaAs, reach even higher FF. Since the conversion efficiency is η = V_ocI_scFF/P_in, FF is the third factor that sets efficiency, alongside voltage and current.

In real cells FF falls below the ideal because of parasitic resistance and recombination. Series resistance consumes voltage near the maximum power point, where the current is large, and flattens the curve on the open-circuit side. A small shunt resistance lets leakage current flow in proportion to voltage and tilts the curve on the short-circuit side. Heavy recombination in the depletion region pushes the ideality factor toward 2, so the curve rises less sharply and FF falls. Because the shape of the I-V curve hints at which loss dominates, FF is also used to diagnose cells.

faq.q: What are typical fill-factor values?
faq.a: Good crystalline silicon cells have values around 0.8, and cells with high open-circuit voltages, such as GaAs, reach higher. If it is well below 0.7, suspect problems such as large series resistance or heavy leakage current.

faq.q: Why is the fill factor never 1?
faq.a: Because of the diode characteristic, in which current changes exponentially with voltage, the current falls gradually as the voltage approaches the open-circuit voltage, so the voltage at the maximum power point is always below the open-circuit voltage and the current always below the short-circuit current.

faq.q: What happens to the fill factor under concentration?
faq.a: The open-circuit voltage rises, so ideally FF rises slightly, but as the current grows the voltage loss IR_s from series resistance increases, so beyond a certain concentration FF falls. Cells for concentration use electrode designs that keep the series resistance small.

ショックレー・クワイサー限界.desc: The upper limit on the conversion efficiency of a single-junction solar cell derived from detailed balance. For AM1.5G it is about 33%, at bandgaps near 1.3–1.4 eV.

about.h: A limit derived from detailed balance
about.p: In 1961 Shockley and Queisser treated the solar cell as a body that absorbs sunlight and emits light at its own temperature, and derived the single-junction efficiency limit from the detailed balance of absorption and emission. The assumptions are that every photon with energy at or above the bandgap is absorbed and creates exactly 1 electron-hole pair, that carriers relax immediately to the band edges, and that the only recombination is unavoidable radiative recombination. It is a fundamental limit that remains even after every loss in a real cell is removed.

about.h: Major losses and the optimum bandgap
about.p: 2 large losses set the limit. Light with energy below the bandgap passes through without being absorbed, and the excess energy of higher-energy photons turns into heat through carrier thermalization. A smaller bandgap absorbs more photons but lowers the voltage per photon, while a larger bandgap raises the voltage but absorbs fewer photons, so the efficiency has an optimum. For the AM1.5G spectrum the maximum of about 33% occurs near 1.3–1.4 eV, and silicon (1.12 eV) also has a bandgap close to the optimum.

The SQ limit applies to a single junction under the assumption of 1 pair per photon, so it can be exceeded by dropping those assumptions. Tandems (multijunctions) that stack cells with different bandgaps reduce thermalization and transmission losses, and with an infinite number of junctions the theoretical limit is about 68% without concentration. Concentrating sunlight raises the open-circuit voltage, and at the maximum concentration set by the sun's apparent size the limit for a single junction becomes about 40%. Multiple exciton generation, in which 1 photon creates several pairs, and hot-carrier cells that extract carriers before they thermalize are also being studied.

faq.q: About what percentage is the SQ limit?
faq.a: For the AM1.5G spectrum the maximum is about 33%, at bandgaps near 1.3–1.4 eV. The value depends on the solar spectrum used and on whether the light is concentrated.

faq.q: Why don't real silicon solar cells reach the SQ limit?
faq.a: Silicon has an indirect gap with slow radiative recombination, so non-radiative recombination such as Auger recombination matters. Losses from reflection, electrode shading, resistance and surface recombination add to this. The theoretical limit for crystalline silicon including Auger recombination is said to be about 29%.

faq.q: Does making a tandem raise the efficiency without limit?
faq.a: Adding junctions raises the limit, but by smaller and smaller amounts. In practice there are trade-offs with current-matching design, losses between layers and manufacturing cost, so configurations of 2 to 3 junctions are the main focus.

タンデム太陽電池.desc: A solar cell that stacks cells with different bandgaps, using short wavelengths in the upper, larger-bandgap cell and long wavelengths in the lower cell. It reduces thermalization and transmission losses.

ペロブスカイト太陽電池.desc: A solar cell that absorbs light in a thin film of metal halide perovskite. It can be made by coating and other low-temperature processes, and its bandgap can be tuned by composition. Stability is a challenge.

エアマス.desc: The path length of sunlight through the atmosphere relative to 1 for overhead sun, roughly 1/cos θ at zenith angle θ. Solar cells are evaluated with the AM1.5G spectrum.
